In particular, high-energy gamma rays from blazars hold significant interest, primarily from those in the flat-spectrum radio quasar (FSRQ) and BL Lac classes of blazars, detected by the Fermi-LAT telescope up to 300 GeV. In the context of astrophysical data analysis, machine learning techniques have become increasingly valuable tools. In this research, a Bayesian neural network classification method is presented, utilizing three handcrafted features to distinguish between blazars and other sources within the Fermi-LAT context. The results indicate an accuracy of up to 93% for both test sets, along with detailed uncertainty assessments for each class within the classification process.

Social media content often shapes public perception, yet social disabilities such as autism spectrum disorder, social anxiety, and ADHD significantly impact individuals' ability to engage with social media platforms. As a result, social content can be discriminatory and excludes certain individuals. To address this gap, researchers have begun to investigate the potential for automated social media moderation. A current study aims to gather input from individuals with social disabilities on their social media experiences. By conducting an online survey, the study seeks to identify the parameters that individuals use to judge social media posts and the support they require to modify their posts. By comprehending how individuals with social disabilities perceive one another, the study aims to provide valuable insights for designing automated moderation systems that enhance social media interactions.

In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations on tensors. We present a case study utilizing symmetric third-order tensors and hypergraphs that are completely multipartite. We investigate the conditions under which a symmetric tensor can be represented as a completely multipartite hypergraph, drawing parallels between the two structures. By doing so, we gain insight into their interconnectedness and complexity. Furthermore, we develop formulas for computing the eigenvalues of the tensor join operation, which is achieved through converting tensors and hypergraphs into matrices. This approach allows us to leverage existing matrix theory results to understand the spectra of tensor joins. We apply our findings to prove the invertibility of certain tensor joins and examine the orthogonality of certain matrix joins associated with tensor joins.

India achieved a groundbreaking success with the deployment of the AstroSat in 2008, marking its entrance into the realm of space-based astronomy. Although this initial effort had limited capabilities, it paved the way for a more advanced satellite to be launched in 2015. Following its completion, a team at the Gravitational Physics High Energy System Laboratory (GPESSL) initiated a project to develop a larger, cutting-edge satellite called the 'INSIST'. This ambitious endeavor aims to maximize scientific potential within a given weight and energy budget, leveraging cutting-edge technology to achieve its objectives. By working across various wavelength ranges, from X-rays to sub-millimeter wavelengths, INSIST will serve multiple scientific community needs. Given its substantial capabilities, INSIST is poised to achieve remarkable breakthroughs across diverse astrophysical domains.

In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and related neurodegenerative diseases, patient outcomes often show irregular patterns. Standard statistical methods that assume a specific time-waiting relationship don't work well when analyzing these irregular changes. A novel approach using natural cubic splines in the mixed effects model has been proposed to handle irregular data patterns in long-term trials. A simulation study confirmed that this method outperforms others in various performance aspects while producing accurate results when assumptions are met. Additionally, we applied this technique to data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative trial, analyzing the effects of PET imaging on patients' disease progression.

A novel computational strategy, named Action-Centered Exploration (ACE), has been developed to pinpoint transition pathways between free energy surfaces. Unlike traditional reaction coordinates focused on geometric properties, the ACE method prioritizes pathways with the greatest action values, which often correspond to the most physically significant mechanisms. Utilizing an energy landscape model, the ACE approach systematically explores free energy space to pinpoint dominant pathways connecting distinct metastable states. In contrast to traditional reaction coordinate-based exploration methods, the ACE strategy more efficiently discovers dominant pathways between free energy surfaces, especially those separated by large free energy barriers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the ACE strategy using a simplified two-bead polymer model, showing its ability to uncover dominant transition pathways between distinct metastable states in the configuration and action spaces.

This study focuses on a parabolic variant of complex Monge-Ampere equations and utilizes a PDE approach to derive the $L^{\infty}$ estimates and subsequent regularity analysis. Several estimates are formulated, proving the necessity of the parabolic structure for the argument. Moreover, various structures are considered to broaden the scope of the results, and the obtained estimates are applied to the study of Hessian equations as well.

Building on a 1991 discovery by Brzozowski and McNaughton, we examine context-free lambda-calculi, a type of enhanced lambda-calculus. Our research reveals that these calculi are precisely defined by a particular category of functions, specifically 2nd degree lambda-definable, language-recognizing superclasses that surpass all regular functions. In addition, our study explores a modified version of the calculi, known as ranked lambda-calculus, which incorporates function symbols with specified arities and determines their usage in terms. We prove that this modified version is precisely recognized by a particular category of generalized automata, specifically ranked lambda-calculi, in conjunction with B\"uchi automata. Furthermore, we investigate several modified versions of these modified versions of the calculi, discovering that each has its distinct corresponding class of recognized languages, providing insights into a hierarchy of computability that surpasses that of regular and context-free languages. Interestingly, each of these modified versions of the calculi experiences a significant reduction in expressiveness when type restrictions are imposed, revealing interesting relationships between the lambda-calculus and monadic second-order logic with specific extensions.

This concise note establishes a relationship between Ito and Stratonovich integrals when conditional measure flows are used as integrands, with the strategic choice of conditional measure flows allowing for a direct, explicit representation of the Wick potential in Stratonovich integrals in terms of the Drift coefficient of the corresponding T martingale problem. This relationship provides a straightforward approach to converting Stratonovich integrals into Ito integrals in the context of conditional measure flows.

This research aims to investigate various types of normal subgroups using a specific topology derived from hull-kernel-type topological spaces. We have made significant contributions by introducing a new class of normal subgroups known as primitive subgroups, examining topological properties such as separation, compactness, connectedness, and continuity in these spaces. Furthermore, our study has provided an alternative perspective on the relationship between topological groups and homomorphisms with continuous mappings among these space types.

This study focuses on cross-domain text-to-sql parsing, which involves teaching models to handle unseen data sources without requiring extensive retraining. The main challenge lies in the cross-domain setting, where text and query data may not align. To address this alignment issue, we propose an auxiliary task during retraining that improves model performance. Our approach outperforms existing baselines on all cross-database evaluations, showcasing its robustness across various databases with different schemas.

Ensuring the safety of individual robots and their interactions within multi-robot systems is of paramount concern, particularly in situations where collisions are difficult to foresee, such as when navigating close to stationary objects or each other. This paper proposes a safe navigation approach for multi-robot systems that effectively manages interactions and risk in dynamic environments through the use of a specialized framework. This framework utilizes a customized formulation of risk-sensitive multi-model predictive control, enabling each robot to make informed decisions that simultaneously achieve collision avoidance and efficient path planning. To tackle the significant computational demands associated with risk-sensitive multi-model formulation, the paper employs the iterated local mapping method and efficiently solves a multi-objective quadratic program. Furthermore, to tackle the issue of communication delays, the paper develops a multi-robot framework that incorporates inter-robot coordination into navigation decisions. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this framework through a series of simulation tests.

Recent data on the Andromeda dwarf galaxy XXV has been examined to determine its mass distribution using a novel method, which accounts for both tidal distortion effects and potential underlying mass clumps. It has been discovered that XXV exhibits an extremely low central dark matter density of approximately 0.05 solar masses per cubic parsec at a confidence level of 95%, effectively ruling out any self-acceleration of its stars. Additionally, a minimum mass profile for XXV has been derived, which, when compared to other known dwarf galaxies in the local universe, including the Canis Major dwarf spheroidal galaxy, indicates a wide range in central dark matter densities.

In massive machine-type communications (mMTC), "grant-free access" offers a significant advantage by eliminating the need for time-consuming signaling procedures. Non-orthogonal access sequences are a key technology in enabling massive connectivity for grant-free systems. However, as the number of users grows, the number of available sequences becomes a major constraint. We propose a two-stage genetic algorithm to design non-orthogonal access sequences for grant-free massive connectivity. The initial stage involves designing a subset of orthogonal sequences, which serve as building blocks for the second stage, where a genetic algorithm is used to create non-orthogonal sequences based on the building blocks generated in the first stage. The simulation results show that the proposed two-stage algorithm achieves better performance while requiring lower computational complexity compared to the single-stage genetic algorithm, with promising applications for mMTC.

A few approaches to approximating the energy exchange between dry and moist air have been applied modelling atmospheric processes. However, the literature lacks a model of dry air specific heat capacity and water substance vaporization/latent heat dependency on temperature and water substance pressure. This research aims to fill this gap by formulating thermodynamically consistent dry air specific heat and latent heat equations and validating them against tabulated water substance thermodynamic data. These equations will then be integrated into a two-fluid model of moist air, with the objective of offering precise and efficient methods for atmospheric thermodynamic calculations.

We introduce algebraic objects, which generalise ordered semirings and monoids, and extend these to objects that include elements acting as negative identities. An exterior algebra analogue is proposed, which provides a cryptomorphism for matroids, and we demonstrate that such a structure achieves a clean, fundamental theorem similar to its matroid counterpart, specifically Gröbner bases.

Research has shown that dialogue state tracking models that account for uncertainty in speech recognition perform better than those that don't, but previous methods of measuring uncertainty, like reliability networks, can interfere with the main network's learning process, limiting performance. We've developed an alternative method using word confusion networks to represent uncertainty, eliminating the need for a separate uncertainty network. Our WCN approach was tested with the Spider dataset, and the results show significant improvements in speech understanding.

We have developed an algorithm to compute the number of torsion-free sheaves on a smooth projective curve, with invariants degree and rank, that have a specified dimension, by breaking down the curve into irreducible components and systematically solving a system of equations for each component, with constraints imposed by junctions between components, and by utilizing the genus information to establish recursive relationships that enable solving of the constraints. The algorithm has been tested and is available in the computer program developed by one of the authors, along with accompanying examples, demonstrating its efficiency in handling complex cases, and we have also formulated a conjecture regarding its computational complexity, which may have implications on the study of Chern characters and Grothendieck groups of torsion-free sheaves on smooth projective curves.

A universal structure encompasses every possible assignment, where the count of satisfying assignments within this structure is computationally difficult to determine accurately. Research has previously identified several families of first-order definable universal structures but it's not known if there's a single universal structure defined within the same logical framework. This study presents two universal structures that can be generated using a limited number of predicate symbols, one utilizing a combination of three binary and three unary predicates and the other utilizing only two binary predicates. Furthermore, we prove that a specific structure defined with only two binary predicates has a limited number of possible expansions using additional binary predicates without increasing the computational complexity of defining elements within the structure.

We propose a strategy for accurately estimating concurrence of mixed states不自发辐射产生的光学量子比特, enabling precise measurement of entanglement in these systems. This method is optimized and capable of achieving the lowest possible error in the estimation of the $f_4$ invariant. We then demonstrate its application in estimating the $f_4$ for various input states and, subsequently, extend it to estimate the upper bound of entanglement in unknown optical qubit states. We achieved the lowest uncertainty in our experiments using optical qubits.

The long-lived palm tree modes (PTMs) observed on the JET tokamak are a distinct type of mode that appears in the edge region and is characterised by its confinement properties, which resemble those of H-modes. The formation mechanism of PTMs is not yet fully understood, but the edge's magnetohydrodynamic instabilities are believed to play a crucial role. In this study, we develop a two-fluid model that incorporates kinetic effects to investigate the formation process of these modes. The model identifies ion temperature gradient (ITG) modes as a primary driver of the formation process, with specific characteristics that align with the experimentally measured properties of PTMs, including their quasi-periodicity and spatial asymmetry. The findings of this study contribute to a deeper understanding of the formation mechanism of these modes, which is crucial for the development of improved plasma control strategies.

We propose a baseline for Continual Learning (CL) by adapting a basic neural network, originally proposed in 2015, and running it on the CLAssical benchmark. Surprisingly, the basic model, despite its simplicity, achieves exceptional results on most evaluated tasks, surpassing more complex models with fewer parameters, such as the one used in the 2018 ImageNet pretraining competition. In fact, the basic model achieves a score of 84.9 in the competition. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that CL tasks are inherently easy for recognition tasks, making them trivial compared to standard image classification benchmarks.

As social media continues to grow, the variety of content being shared has expanded to include not just text, but also images and videos, necessitating multi-modal computing capabilities.  Due to the limited availability of training data for social media content, especially in identifying inappropriate posts, researchers have started to employ pre-trained neural networks for visual and audio features to supplement their language models.  Nonetheless, our analysis of hate speech classification techniques has revealed an important consideration: enhancing the understanding of how decisions are made within these models.  By incorporating human expertise in identifying hateful content, we've developed an innovative approach to augmenting existing training data and applied it to a unique interpreter built from a combination of neural and rule-based systems.  Moreover, our investigation highlights the significance of appropriately handling missing visual data in hate speech classification by comparing our own strategy to simply using a placeholder image.  Our study also examines the impact of employing Bayesian neural networks on improving the interpretability of deep learning models for hate speech classification by revealing the underlying connections between input features and predicted labels.  Our proposed techniques for enhancing hate speech classification have produced exceptional results on a prominent benchmark dataset, surpassing the existing state-of-the-art by approximately one percentage point in accuracy, while also providing an understandable and transparent classifier that reveals its own decision-making process.

We investigate the behavior of large networks of theta neurons,  with connections based on random patterns. By using analytical and numerical methods, we examine how the distribution of neuron connection probabilities affects synchronization within the network. Our research shows that synchronization is highly dependent on which neuron subgroups the highly connected neurons are part of. By utilizing a newly developed method that approximates complex network structures with simpler, uniform models, we gain insight into the complex interplay between neuron synchronization and network connectivity.

Recent years have seen the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) in Automatic Program Repair (APR) models that generate code. This work proposes an innovative extension of the APR framework with a novel adversarial module based on patch generation, which functions as a discriminator to validate whether the generated code patches are high-quality. This module is trained and improved concurrently with the generator, thereby producing more accurate and reliable patches. A comparison of the proposed method against top-performing APR models on 12 widely-used benchmarks demonstrates the superiority of the developed approach, particularly in a setting with limited positive examples. Moreover, the proposed method's effectiveness is also demonstrated on positive-example-rich datasets like JavaCodeRepository, showing comparable results. The source code and experiments can be accessed at https://github.com/101ye/AdvPatchGAN.

This study introduces a general framework for the capacity region of a complex interference channel with interconnected user pairs, characterized by a multidimensional output and separate inputs from each pair. We derive an exact capacity region expression based on this framework, and provide an inner bound using the finite alphabet GIFC capacity result by Han and Khanduri as a reference. Further analysis is conducted on a specific binary interference channel with OR operations at the receivers to verify the proposed bounds.

We are developing multi-dimensional algorithms for analyzing flow measurements in heavy-ion collisions.  These algorithms, such as flow decomposition and the Hough-mass technique, can effectively reconstruct anisotropic flow up to at least the 5th order (with five spatial dimensions involved).  This enhanced decomposition approach leverages orthonormal polynomials to improve mass and collision geometry resolution.  Furthermore, our novel Hough-mass technique offers a more detailed and model-independent examination of flow measurement data, with applications to studies of Equation-of-State (EOS) and the phase diagram.  This technique utilizes a 3-dimensional flow vector (an extension of 2-dimensional vectors developed by the ALICE collaboration) to explore various EOS scenarios in a model-independent manner.  This technique has been successfully implemented using data from central Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at a laboratory energy of 200 GeV.

Early detection of COVID-19 is a highly challenging task, and the risk of misdiagnosis is significant. In this research, a new, privacy-conscious, and efficient deep learning model for identifying COVID-19 is developed, combining early detection and adversarial training. The proposed neural network model, AdversialCNN, is built on convolutional neural networks and incorporates three advanced techniques: Squeeze and Excitation, Residual connections, and Adversarial Training. The Squeeze and Excitation component enables the CNN to focus on crucial features while mitigating the risk of leaking sensitive data. The Residual connections facilitate efficient computational processes and enable AdversialCNN to function effectively even when trained on limited datasets. The final technique, Adversarial Training, enables AdversialCNN to identify COVID-19 cases more accurately and efficiently. The cross-experiment results demonstrate that AdversialCNN achieves impressive outcomes, boasting high recall and a low false positive rate, and surpassing existing models across various datasets, particularly the massive De-COVID2, showcasing its capabilities in early detection and accurate diagnosis of COVID-19.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture capable of addressing complex graph-based problems, including VBC problem outcomes. However, implementing GNNs in wireless communication systems poses significant computational and communication overheads. To mitigate this, a decentralized inference approach has been developed, which involves splitting both computation and communication across multiple devices. This solution is generically applicable to a wide range of neural network architecture inductions, not just GNNs. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed decentralized method reduces processing and data transmission latency by as much as 75% and 92% respectively, when compared to the current best practices.

The high prevalence of violence worldwide is a persistent concern.  In the Brazilian state of Goias, homicide rates fluctuate significantly, primarily linked to drug trafficking.  Our study analyzed the trends in G\xf3ias's homicide rates from 2002 to 2014, based on data from the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics.  Using correlation analysis, we categorized municipalities into groups with similar levels of violence.  Our findings suggest that the high homicide rates in Goias are closely related to drug trafficking and its influence on the region.

Our approach modifies stochastic gradient descent by developing noise-adaptive and problem-adaptive variations of gradient descent. Specifically, a new estimator is introduced to adaptively estimate local Hessian eigenvalues, enabling effective noise cancellation. The estimated eigenvalues are then applied as preconditioners in gradient descent. Through theoretical proof and numerical validation, we demonstrate that this novel estimator converges to the true Hessian eigenvalues, even in noisy conditions. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical convergence guarantee for the preconditioned gradient descent and show that it can significantly reduce iteration counts by carefully balancing noise and step size. Additionally, we find that a two-time-scale accelerated gradient descent can achieve better convergence rates than the preconditionized version.

Axion-like particles (ALPs) are promising candidates for dark matter and can resolve the strong CP problem. The baby IAXO detector will search for evidence of ALPs within solar flux, which can provide significant evidence for the ALP dark matter theory. It can also reveal the properties of ALPs, such as their axion-photon and photon-photophoton couplings. These features can be determined with high confidence, making them a key aspect of the ALP dark matter model.

The occupation number over the plasma cutoff is derived for a plasma with electrons having non-uniform energy, which includes cases of self-oscillating systems based on charged particles in an electromagnetic field and a potential barrier. These systems can be conceptualized as particles bouncing between the potential minimum and a barrier that is slowly changing in amplitude and frequency, with the occupation number at frequencies near the oscillation frequency being close to either 0 or infinity for low-frequency and high-frequency ranges, respectively. This enables estimation of the occurrence probability of charged particle motion types that result in electromagnetic radiation emission or incoherent movement, enabling identification of electromagnetic waves in in vacuum produced by such self-oscillating systems in at least one frequency range, with further investigation of emission at high frequencies deferred to a separate study.

Developing a reliable and versatile grasping system for robots is a substantial challenge.
To overcome this hurdle, a large and diverse training dataset is needed.
Existing datasets, however, are limited in scope, hindering the creation of advanced grasping systems.
We propose an extensive dataset featuring large-scale simulation data.
Our dataset includes over 100,000 different objects from over 10,000 unique categories and more than 100,000 successful dexterous grasp attempts from three different robots.
Our dataset can significantly accelerate the creation of sophisticated grasping systems by providing training data.
Our dataset is available for research at https://dexgraspnet.github.io.

A novel approach is introduced to incorporate motion compensation (MC) into free-breathing, oblique axial abdominal MRI sequences, specifically turbo spin-echo (TSE) and turbo spin-echo turbo echo-planar imaging (TSE-TSE). The method employs radial in-and-out k-space sampling to track organ movement and reorders the data in the azimuthal direction during reconstruction, thereby facilitating accurate image reconstruction. The method's parameters are optimized to accommodate large movements, potentially arising from a combination of respiration and organ displacement, by adjusting trajectory sampling intervals between projections, in conjunction with MC. The free-breathing approach's efficacy is evaluated using three volunteers and four subjects, comparing it to free-breathing MC-TSE/TSE-TSE images to standard single-shot spin-echo (SSSE) reference images acquired with a longer scan time. The results show that the proposed sequence produces high-quality images, comparable in quality to SSSE images, while reducing the scan time to 20-30 minutes. The novel approach enables the acquisition of high-quality diagnostic free-breathing MRI images, facilitating tumor detection, dosimetry, and respiratory functional imaging in abdominal and pelvic regions.

Model compression via knowledge distillation has become a widely used method for accelerating the inference process of deep learning models. However, previous studies have mainly focused on transferring knowledge from a large pre-trained model to a smaller target model without considering the preservation of information flow within the target model. As a result, the given layer range and network structure of the target model often limit its ability to learn and optimize its parameters, leading to suboptimal model compression outcomes. In this paper, we explore and quantify the impact of information flow preservation on model compression from theoretical and empirical perspectives. Building on this foundation, we introduce InDistill, a novel model compression method that involves preserving information flow within specific layers. Our results demonstrate that InDistill outperforms previous models on several tasks.

We establish specific sufficient conditions based on a submersion's behavior similar to linear functions, under which topological equivalence of the submersion implies topological foliation equivalence. Notably, our results show that for certain families of linear-like functions, topological foliation equivalence can be derived from submersion equivalence. Additionally, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a canonical topological foliation equivalent to the given family of foliations.

Ecosystems that thrive in arid regions are particularly susceptible to degradation caused by overgrazing, a prevalent issue in developing nations where animal husbandry is a primary economic activity. To simulate vegetation dynamics in response to overgrazing in such areas, we employed a non-local grazing model that assumes animals move away from densely vegetated areas and towards sparsely vegetated areas. Our study reveals that increasing non-locality tends to stabilize the ecosystem, with results also varying according to the specific grazing intensity employed.

A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to estimate the properties of high-dimensional vectors, specifically focusing on finding the heaviest or lightest items. The CountSketch method has been extensively studied and validated for scenarios where adversaries have limited control over the process, but its behavior in scenarios where adversaries have complete control over the process remains less clear. We discovered that in scenarios where adversaries can adapt their choices, even slight increases in the randomness level can result in significant performance degradation for CountSketch, specifically its ability to achieve a certain level of accuracy. We discovered that merely increasing the level of randomness by a small margin can result in a substantial gap between the minimum CountSketch performance and its performance under optimal conditions, with this gap increasing exponentially as certain parameters approach their theoretical limits. We also found similar vulnerabilities in other randomized linear measurement techniques used to find the heaviest or lightest items, with their performance under adversarial conditions also exhibiting significant gaps. We further demonstrated the existence of efficient algorithms that can exploit weaknesses in both CountSketch and other randomized linear measurement techniques used to find the heaviest or lightest items, with these algorithms capable of accurately predicting outcomes with a certain level of accuracy. We also found similar vulnerabilities in the use of purely random linear measurements for estimating functions, with their performance under adversarial conditions also exhibiting significant gaps. We also found similar vulnerabilities in the use of linear measurements based on independent and identically distributed observations for estimating functions, with their performance under adversarial conditions also

A python-based program called ipie has been created for auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations, along with its accompanying package, ipie. AFQMC is an inherently elementary method for ground-state many-body problems in ab initio computational chemistry and physics. The ipie package enables extensive flexibility and efficiency on both central processing units and graphical processing units, facilitating seamless integration with pre-existing, C-based quantum chemistry software packages, such as PySCF. This collaboration allows users to conduct ab initio calculations with ipie within the traditional quantum chemistry framework. Furthermore, ipie provides comprehensive functionality, making it an all-inclusive auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo program.

High-frequency trading, a contentious yet lucrative practice, utilizes advanced algorithms and swift decision-making processes to give investors a substantial advantage. By leveraging rapid computational capabilities, traders can swiftly analyze market dynamics and execute strategies based on differing game outcomes. Now, researchers are exploring the potential of quantum computing in creating a groundbreaking "quantum Prisoner's Dilemma," aiming to showcase the power of quantum algorithms in high-speed market environments. This investigation involves investigating several quantum game algorithms on the IBM Q API server. Furthermore, findings are analyzed from the perspective of an experienced investor, taking into account real-world constraints such as communication delays between the game interface and IBM servers, which are expected to impact trading performance.

We examine a mechanism design problem where an agent, or "intermediary," claims to sell an item to a seller for a price, but actually wants to maximize their own profit, not the seller's, under a valuation model where the item's value to the seller is independent but randomly determined. Specifically, we focus on a scenario where the item's value is drawn from a known distribution and demonstrate that mechanisms can be designed to achieve nearly optimal expected revenue in a two-agent scenario and within a constant factor of expected revenue in a multi-agent scenario with numerous intermediaries. A crucial step in our approach involves a "black-box transformation" that creates a new mechanism without requiring a detailed understanding of the intermediaries' motives.

To facilitate abstractive summarization, we've developed an automated planning system 
that utilizes prompt-like vector representations, known as entity prompts, for 
identifying content to incorporate into a generated summary. After pre-training 
with frequent words from sums of datasets, these prompts can be incorporated into 
models and fine-tuned task-specifically, and our results demonstrate that they can 
effectively represent content to be recapitulated when combined with existing 
summarization models such as PERSEUS, a generated-content based model, and 
BERT-based models like BART and T5.

This research validates differentiability theorems for a multivariate function where each variable can be reordered, given that the function's partial derivatives are continuous. It involves leveraging known partial derivatives and applying the Mean Value Theorem to establish the theorem. Additionally, the study provides new theorems for comparing the n-th partial derivative with a sum of (n-1)-partial derivatives in a neighborhood. These theorems offer simplified proofs for existing theorems in mathematical analysis.

Human vocal synchronization in social interactions indicates deep connection and shared understanding. To assess this phenomenon accurately, we require reliable, automated, context-sensitive tools capable of extracting relevant information from complex speech patterns. Our approach involves a novel model developed using machine learning that analyzes spoken language in social dialogues to quantify vocal synchronization. By leveraging extensive labeled data, this model demonstrates superior performance compared to its alternatives, providing a more accurate measurement of this essential aspect of human connection.

A recent study applied a full sound and complete framework for a quantum control language to the unitary sphere, revealing the existence of a richer structure within this domain.  It is known that a certain substructure of the unitary sphere, denoted as U(n), has a corresponding full sound complete quantum control language called U(n)^.  This paper proposes the existence of an even more intricate substructure of U(n)^, denoted as Lambda(n)^, which would be full sound complete for a designated subset of a universal quantum control language.  It already had a sound complete categorical model for this language called Lambda, and the study aims to show that a sound complete quantum control language called Lambda(n) would have a similar categorical model for the category Lambda(n)^.  It would also show that the proposed substructure of U(n)^, denoted as Lambda(n)^, is contained within a larger, yet known, substructure of U(n)^, which is another proposed substructure, Lambda(n)^, and that the containment is strict unless n equals 1.

Analytical calculations have been performed for two types of multi-body form factors, 
corresponding to two-quasiparticle and an electron-hole pair in systems of fractional quantum Hall interactions. 
These computations have been carried out both numerically and symbolically, and the results show excellent 
agreement with previous Monte Carlo simulations and quantum Monte Carlo data for form factor norms. 
Furthermore, the known asymptotic behavior of the form factors at large distances has been successfully 
reproduced.

In the context of glaciology, particularly when modeling contact problems at ice beds, Stokes variational inequalities emerge. A semicoercive type of variational inequality is derived from a particular situation, and we investigate the Stokes variational inequality, focusing on its coercive part's right-hand side, and its finite element approximation, given that the problem involves infinite domains and is thus subject to truncation and boundary conditions. An error estimate is presented for the finite element approximation, given assumptions about the problem domain, boundary conditions, and finite element spaces. Furthermore, we solve the problem in two dimensions using the virtual element method and illustrate the findings with numerical results.

Recent research suggests that galaxy feedback from powerful outflows is a key factor in limiting star formation. However, the specific characteristics of these powerful outflows, such as their speed and mass, are still unclear. A study using data from a high-resolution VLT/X-shooter observation of a starbursting galaxy, NGC 253, has provided new insights into this question. By combining VLT/X-shooter data with theoretical models, researchers found that a fast-moving outflow in NGC 253 has a significant impact on regulating star formation. A strong wind from the galaxy's center is found to suppress star formation, with the outflow's speed and mass consistent with powerful outflows observed in other starbursting galaxies. These findings support the idea that galaxy feedback from galactic-scale outflows is a crucial factor in galaxy formation and evolution.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. We discovered that the initial transverse geometry significantly influences the triangular flow in these systems. In contrast, the pressure gradient and parton scattering within the quark-gluon phase, hadron resonance phase, and freeze-out process all have relatively minor effects on the triangular flow in these specific collisions.

We propose a novel, unified framework that synchronizes human and robotic team performance. Motivated by the limitations of existing tests, which typically evaluate humans and robots in isolation, this framework addresses these shortcomings by creating a common test bed. It is built on the dual principles of shared adaptability and reciprocal communication. In line with adaptive team theory, it posits that effective teams adjust their communication and actions based on the available information. By embodying these guiding principles for both human and robotic participants, this synchronous framework provides a common standard for assessing and comparing the capabilities of robotic systems with their human counterparts. It further facilitates the development of evaluation tools, including metrics and benchmarks, that can be applied to assess adaptive teamwork.

Deep neural network models for semantic segmentation are typically trained using satellite imagery, but their success heavily relies on large, annotated datasets. To improve this process, researchers have proposed pre-training models using a self-supervised approach that doesn't require labeled data. A new study investigates the effectiveness of depth pre-training for semantic segmentation in outdoor satellite imagery, specifically focusing on the impact of scale and the role of image resolution. By analyzing these aspects, the study sheds light on the use of pre-trained models and highlights the benefits of a hybrid approach that combines pre-trained and fine-tuned models. The study's results demonstrate that pre-training using a self-supervised depth model can yield improved semantic segmentation results, with a specific image tile size of 256x256 pixels being the most effective for this purpose.

Let's consider the class of log-harmonic mappings from the unit disk to the complex plane, where a logarithmic Laplacian equation is applied. We have improved the Bohr radius for the class of starlike log-harmonic mappings by providing a bound under certain conditions on the coefficients of the mapping's power series expansion. Specifically, for such mappings, we have shown that the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of the logarithmic representation does not exceed one-half the sum of the first powers of the disk's variable, under the condition that the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of the logarithmic representation can be bounded for sufficiently small values of the disk's variable, specifically $0<\tau<1$. For mapping functions satisfying this bound, we have determined the exact value of the Bohr radius, which is given as $\frac{1+\tau}{2}+\ln(1+\tau)-\frac{1+\tau}{2}\ln(1+\tau)^2$. Our results represent an advancement on the existing literature, particularly for $\tau=0.31407$, where we have recovered a more recent value for the Bohr radius, closely aligned with numerical estimates at $0.31555$.

A nonparametric measure of correlation known as Kendall's tau is examined, along with an efficient method for estimating its value from data. The proposed method significantly reduces computational time by adapting a standard approach, allowing for quicker calculations when dealing with larger datasets. The modified approach specifically identifies key components in its underlying Hájek projection, leading to a notable runtime improvement for fixed-dimension datasets.

The integration of edge intelligence technology within the edge computing infrastructure has enabled intelligent decision-making capabilities for vehicles in complex traffic scenarios. Despite this advancement, concerns regarding user privacy persist when sharing vehicle data with EI nodes. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for implementing privacy-protective edge intelligence applications in vehicular networks. Firstly, a survey is presented on various privacy-preserving edge intelligence techniques, particularly for vehicles. Subsequently, a framework is designed to evaluate privacy, reliability, latency, energy efficiency, and cost factors associated with different local differential privacy models when applied to Vehicular Edge Intelligence scenarios. By comparing available privacy-preserving EI techniques using metrics like privacy loss, execution time, accuracy, and energy efficiency, numerical results demonstrate that a framework utilizing local differential privacy mechanisms along with real-time vehicle trajectory data achieves an optimal balance between privacy protection and task accuracy. Furthermore, experiments indicate that increasing data granularities enhances an EI node's ability to generalize training data, thereby providing a reliable mechanism for protecting user data in privacy-sensitive Vehicular Edge Intelligence scenarios.

This study focuses on the application of the Euler characteristic for advanced topological data analysis in multi-dimensional spaces. Building upon its successful 1-dimensional use in computing persistence, the 2-dimensional approach is now being developed to identify features on complex surfaces by solving partial differential equations. The Euler characteristic serves as a primary invariant, often paired with the Morse function in our models, enabling the calculation of surfaces' areas in the process. The current research involves developing theory and methods for efficient computations, utilizing a novel multi-step framework to break down surfaces into manageable components. This framework utilizes a novel structure called a 2-persistence module, along with a newly proposed measure of the 'size' of local data sets through a specific norm. The framework also incorporates innovative mathematical tools such as a 2-dimensional analog of the Reeb graph and tree thickenings for effective computations.

Our analysis involves examining the existence, stability, and long-term predictions of all six possible types of Holling-Tanner predation models that feature a strong Allee effect in the prey population and a type III functional response, as well as four models with a type II functional response. Additionally, stability diagrams are developed for each model with type III functional response, and stability switches are identified in relation to changes in time delay within the prey's growth term. This investigation also explores how time delay impacts the existence of oscillations in population patterns, and our examination of parameter sets reveals that coexisting steady states can lead to coexisting cycles in populations of prey and predator.

The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory proposing that the graph of a polytope with $d$ dimensions and $n$ constraints would have at most $n-d+1$ steps between any two vertices. This hypothesis, proven false by Santos, led to a modified conjecture by Bohnenberg, which suggested that the facet pivot method of the simplex algorithm cannot be longer than $n-d+1+O(d)$ steps for a $d$ dimensional polytope with $n$ constraints. This article proves one part of this revised conjecture for a specific case where the difference between the number of constraints and dimensions is much smaller than the dimension itself. Specifically, it shows that for a $d$ dimensional polytope with $n$ constraints, the facet pivot method of the simplex algorithm is at most $n-d+1+O(n^{d/2}d)$ steps, which improves the previous known iteration bound of $O(nd 2^{d})$ by de Kogge and Tiemann.

We explore in an associative ring R with identity, the scarcity of k-torsion in the NK1GQ(R), which are Bass nil-groups for general and unitary quadratic groups. Building on a graded version of Quillen-Suslin theory, we establish an analogous concept for graded rings.

This paper undertakes a thorough comparison of the comprehensive, off-shell computation for pp -> ttj events, particularly focusing on the dileptonic decay channel, with an approximation based on the narrow width assumption. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the shape of the invariant mass distribution m(tt) in events featuring a single lepton, ultimately determining their potential impact in top quark mass measurements. To facilitate precise comparisons with experimental data, we develop a specialized tool that breaks down the m(tt) distribution into various components, encompassing the one-loop correction to the resonant reduction, the reduction itself, as well as the integration of off-shell and non-resonant parts. This tool is built using a combination of analytical and numerical methods of perturbation theory, particularly in the context of the Standard Model. Applying our developed tool to the ATLAS and CMS data from a 2016, 13 TeV proton-proton collision, we observe notable discrepancies in the m(tt) shape, with off-shell and non-resonant contributions accounting for approximately 5-10% at low m(tt) values and up to 10% at the spectrum's tail, which could introduce biases in extracted top quark masses.

In the realm of biometric security, researchers have been exploring zero-shot deep learning approaches to detect facial spoofing attacks. A novel framework utilizing Transfer Learning and feature representation techniques is proposed, employing various pre-trained Transformers and Convolutional Neural Networks, along with ensemble methods. This approach achieved a high level of success on the WU-VERS, Celeb-SP, and List of Real and Fake Samples benchmarks, boasting zero-shot performance rates of 93.3%, 98.13%, and 98.53% respectively, outperforming recent state-of-the-art zero-shot models by a significant margin.

Deep reinforcement learning has emerged as a prominent technique for resolving dynamic decision-making challenges in numerous domains. Its application in autonomous driving is particularly significant, given the diverse range of tasks it can address. Nonetheless, implementing deep reinforcement learning solutions poses considerable difficulties, given their complexities and disparities. Researchers have developed an integrated framework for applying deep reinforcement learning to autonomous driving problems, designed to leverage the collaborative nature of various deep reinforcement learning algorithms and streamline their implementation. This framework addresses several challenges faced by deep reinforcement learning practitioners, including defining states, actions, and rewards, and optimizing policy learning through indirect model training. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness by resolving multiple tasks within an simulated autonomous driving environment, ultimately showing that it can achieve superior results through streamlined design.

Evolutionary algorithms have seen significant advancements through the integration of parallel processing capabilities, enabling the execution of generations across multiple cores within a short timeframe. Nevertheless, the lack of synchronization in these parallel environments can lead to suboptimal parent selection, allowing fitter individuals to overtake slower counterparts, ultimately impeding algorithm performance. To address this limitation, our research proposes a novel parent selection method for the Parallel Evolutionary Multi-Objective Algorithm (PEMOA), an asynchronous parallel optimization algorithm, aiming to minimize the impact of time-related bias on its performance. Building upon PEMOA, a frequency-based parent selection technique was introduced to optimize evaluation time fairness, resulting in a notable improvement in solution quality and convergence speed, as confirmed through extensive numerical testing and an application in the real-world context of parameter tuning for the LightGBM model in Keras.

The initial microlensing analysis of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, conducted with the IR telescope, identified a planet-hosting lens mass ratio around 0.003 and a projected planet separation of 1.19 AU. Data collected with the Keck NIR camera confirmed the mass ratio, allowing the lensed mass to be calculated as 0.00120 +/- 0.000024 M_L. This leads to a mass estimate for the lensed object, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, ranging from 9.8 to 16.4 M_Earth. Observations also show the lensed object, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434, has a temperature of 387.5 K and a luminosity of 2.24 x 10^-7 L_Sun. An analysis of the microlensing data also allows the calculation of the lensed object's host star mass as 0.42 M_Sun and its luminosity as 0.12 L_Sun. This results in a metallicity of -0.21 Z_Zun for the host star.

The concept of an effective, time-independent Hamiltonian is extended to a broader class of quantum dynamics with periodic coefficients, encompassing both unitary and non-productive Lindbladians. By addressing the impact of noise on fast oscillating control pulses in NISQ-era quantum computing, we develop high-frequency expansions for periodic quantum dynamics. Our work generalizes Edmonds' 1960 method for deriving exchange Hamiltonians to a non-rotating frame and more complex scenarios. Furthermore, we present a new proof demonstrating the under certain conditions the independence of first-order expansion coefficients from the noise level, which is particularly advantageous for experimentalists. This achievement is also significant as it resolves an issue identified in Exner et al.'s 2022 research by Exner, Gouraud, and Smilga. Ultimately, we establish novel bounds on the truncation error of high-frequency expansions, which is an essential resource for researchers studying this topic.

Our study of the ferromagnetic and spin freezing behavior in the $cepd_{1-x}rh_x$ ($0\le x\le 1$) material used small-angle neutron scattering and depolarization techniques. We observed that x-$\approx$0.5 is a critical point where both phenomena occur. To investigate the underlying cause, we examined the flux distribution in the small-angle range. Our analysis revealed a higher flux level near $q=0$ for $x\le 0.5$ in comparison to $x\ge 0.5$. These results suggest that $x\approx 0.5$ corresponds to a state where the material transitions from small-sized ferromagnetic domains to frozen clusters.

A massive star-forming area, G176.51+00.20, located 12.3 kpc away in the Galactic Centre, is predicted to house numerous high-mass stars. Using the 11-m and 25-m Parkes radio telescope, researchers observed narrow-line self-absorptions (SLSAs) in the neutral hydrogen (HI) emission at 41.66 MHz toward this source. A total of 14 SLSAs were detected, 11 of which were observed for the first time. The researchers determined the properties of these SLSAs, such as their optical depth, absorption width, and column density. A comparison with other star-forming regions revealed similarities and differences in the SLSAs. A possible explanation for the formation of SLSAs is provided, along with suggestions for further research.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all positive real numbers $\beta > 1$ that satisfy $\beta^2 - \beta - 1 = 0$ to those in the range $1 < \beta' \leq 2$, where $\beta'$ has a greedy expansion $\theta_{\beta'} = (t_0, t_1, \dots, t_k, 1, 1, \dots, 1)$, with the length of the repeating sequence of 1s being at least 2. This proof relies on techniques from topological conjugacy in beta-shifts. To support our results, we also provide previously known methods for efficiently computing the greedy expansion of $\beta$.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 3.03 fb^-1 of data, our study utilized CP properties of muon pairs from nearly 290,000 suppressed charm meson pairs and approximately 360,000 unsuppressed charm meson pairs to analyze their relationships. These analyses yielded a derived phi_s value of sin(phi_s) = sin(0.03 rad) +/- 0.12 rad, combining statistical and systematic uncertainties, and a similar result for anti-particle decays. Combining these results produced a final phi_s value of 0.07 rad with a total uncertainty of 0.11 rad, which is in line with the Standard Model prediction.

Deep Neural Networks have excelled in various image classification tasks.
Their adaptability is a major advantage, but their reliance on well-trained datasets is also a major limitation.
Techniques for domain adaptation allow the knowledge gained from training datasets to be effectively applied even when they differ in nature from other related datasets.
This paper compares domain adaptation methods for image classification.
We use two well-known datasets, CIFAR and Visem, for our analysis.
Our findings indicate that domain adaptation methods can significantly enhance the performance of Deep Neural Networks on unrelated datasets.
The results also show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CIFAR dataset, outperforming existing techniques.
An open-source implementation of our results is available on GitHub.

In finite fields, specific types of points known as affine arcs are defined. Notably, points along non-horizontal lines in $\mathbb F_q^2$ form a maximal set of affine arcs. To the best of our knowledge, the exact number of maximum affine arcs within $\mathbb F_q^2$ has yet to be determined. However, we establish a precise lower bound for this count, which equals $\sum_{k=2}^{q}k(q-k)$, achieved through a modified application of Berlekamp's method. Moreover, we establish corresponding upper and lower bounds for the number of maximum affine arcs within projective space $\mathbb F_q^3$.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in an $n$-regular triangle, where it is also demonstrated that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ four-element subsets represented by a downward-pointing triangle in a triangular structure.

Generating explanations for predictions in Machine Learning models is becoming increasingly essential in areas like healthcare and law, where understanding the reasoning behind predictions is vital for trust and safety. The development of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for complex data analysis has been significant, but existing methods of explaining their predictions are limited. We present the Parameterized Explainer (PEX), a novel technique that offers both local and global explanations by analyzing variations in GNN parameters. Using experiments on public datasets, PEX effectively identifies key nodes and contrasts the impact of their different roles in GNNs, outperforming existing exploration methods.

The nature of radiation from galaxy clusters remains a contentious issue. The X-ray emission in these objects is believed to originate from the interaction of relativistic electrons with extragalactic magnetic fields, a process that also generates radio emission. The study of emission from galaxy clusters at X-ray energies can thus provide valuable insights into their evolution. As part of this investigation, the peculiar object RXCJ0232.2-4420 was examined. The cluster exhibits both X-ray and radio emission properties, and its two central galaxies, NGC4426 and NGC4438, are thought to be the source of these emissions. By analyzing 2MASS data, it was found that the cluster members share a common distance from Earth. The X-ray spectrum of the object was modeled using thermal plasma, and it was found that these emissions were consistent with high-temperature gas resulting from supernovae activity. The gas was also found to be in a state of motion, and this movement was likely caused by the interaction of jets produced by the galaxies' supermassive black holes. The study further revealed that the X-ray emission in the cluster was not uniform, and that it was characterized by higher-temperature gas in the gas-poor regions. The study also detected radio galaxies within the X-ray cluster, and it was found that these galaxies exhibit distinct characteristics.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a type of recurrent neural network,
has garnered significant attention due to its superior performance in various
tasks. Like its earlier counterpart, the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), the LMU
incorporates a memory module to process sequential data. In recent research,
a parallelization method for learning the LMU's weight parameters was
proposed to overcome its inherent serial computation limitation. In this work,
we challenge and disprove the claimed parallelism of the previous approach.
Furthermore, we establish a theoretical basis for our critique and propose an
alternative method to determine the degree of parallelism in LMU training.
Supported by empirical evidence, our method yields performance comparable to
the previously reported results.

Our current understanding of the Standard Model (SM) seems to be an incomplete picture, as it fails to address fundamental questions regarding dark matter and neutrino masses.  The leading theories proposed to fill these gaps often predict the existence of particles interacting with ordinary matter at extremely low rates.  The search for such particles beyond the SM has become a major focus for the community, particularly for sub-eV weakly-interacting particles classified as feebley-interacting particles.  The research aims to identify these particles at quantum field theoretical consistency points, which could significantly impact the development of new models to address the limitations of the SM, as well as inform the design of future experiments.  The search for FI particles involves exploring a range of existing and upcoming experimental setups, with a goal to expand the limited possibilities of detection and identify potential areas of breakthrough.  The research will be divided into three distinct mass ranges to facilitate the comparison of results from different experiments, covering particle masses below 1 keV, between 1-100 keV, and 100-1 MeV.  The presentation will provide an overview of searches for particles predicted by various new physics models, particularly those involving the Higgs portal and light boson mediators, as well as light neutrinos, covering past, present, and future experimental setups.

Language is a complex system characterized by the dynamic interplay between its elements.  Traditionally, research has centered on aspects of language such as its composition and communication methods.  In contrast, a new line of investigation is now exploring the development of language's overall coherence.  By employing a modified version of the naming game, a novel measure of language coherence has been devised that evaluates a population's language complexity based on its length and structural characteristics.  Results indicate that when a population exhibits a high degree of coherence, this is often the result of a limited number of long words and a high degree of word repetition.  Moreover, it's been discovered that when a population is mobile, a significant level of coherence often emerges, whereas in a non-migratory population, coherence often dissipates.  Moreover, a population's rate of word creation and the level of noise within the communication process have a significant impact on language coherence, particularly when a population is mobile.  In contrast, when a population is not mobile, language coherence tends to be lower, particularly when there is a high level of noise within the communication process.

PINN algorithms have achieved remarkable success in solving various problems governed by partial differential equations. Their ability to find solutions to inverse problems and transmit information across long distances has made them a preferred choice. Nevertheless, their tendency to exhibit "spectral bias" leads to poor outcomes when dealing with irregular data patterns, as they heavily rely on high-frequency information. To counter this issue, we investigated the impact of adding momentum in the gradient descent optimization process for PINN and discovered that it significantly reduces the effect of spectral bias. Our findings show that momentum facilitates neural networks to learn from both low- and high-frequency information within PDEs, leading to notable improvements in spectral tests. Additionally, we found that PINN models incorporating momentum demonstrate better performance in solving inverse problems and provide an opportunity for understanding the behavior of neural networks in learning from PDE data.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval $(0,1)$ where one end is subject to Kelvin-Voigt damping over a limited area, with a separate boundary condition applied to the other end. Our results demonstrate that under suitable parameters the asymptotic behavior of solutions results in total decay with a rate that is weak (polynomial) rather than optimal (exponential). The weak decay rate is a direct consequence of the lack of observability for the backwave in the undamped segment of the domain, which can be understood through the transmission conditions linking the two waves.

Recent research has demonstrated that reinforcement learning agents can reach human-level performance in complex tasks. However, the ability to understand and explain the decision-making process of these agents remains a significant challenge, particularly when dealing with dynamic and uncertain environments. Current model-free methods struggle to accurately capture these processes, resulting in the inability to provide interpretable models. To address this issue, we propose a high-level interpretation framework using Inductive Logic Programming, allowing us to derive and utilize high-level rules that can be employed in designing a hierarchical model for agent decision-making. This approach, known as IHoME, leverages these rules to create task-specific subgoals and policies that facilitate efficient and effective agent learning and adaptation to novel situations.

We've developed an all-optical technique for generating asymmetric transmission of optical tones by exploiting the quantum properties of a squeezed vacuum field. By adjusting the squeeze angle of the quantum field, it's feasible to create N-port nonreciprocal devices capable of directing light in a specific direction towards Port N. Our method also enables the creation of switchable nonreciprocal devices, which can be controlled by modifying the squeeze angle. Furthermore, we've found that the directionality of our all-optical scheme can be enhanced by combining it with conventional nonreciprocal schemes used in quantum communication techniques.

We introduce a summation operator and establish a summand selection theorem,
which facilitates the generalization of several sum-of-translates functions,
including a more comprehensive interpretation of the arithmetical mean
associated with additive number theory. Moreover, we investigate Fenton-like
extremal problems for these functions, deriving formulas utilizing summand
selection, as well as rough estimates that encompass explicit numerical bounds.
Our analysis encompasses cases involving multiple summand lengths, providing
computationally accessible and accurate approximations for the summand
selection problem. The formulas developed not only recover previous results but
also yield improved estimates in comparison to existing literature. The discussion
is supplemented with open conjectures and problems.

The CRESST experiment, a direct dark matter detection initiative, will examine the interactions involving $^6$Li and dark matter within the energy range of 6-100 MeV. By doing so, it will be able to test the effectiveness of spin-dependent nuclear cross-sections for PMNS and fermion dark matter particles with strengths of $10^{-40}$ to $10^{-36}$ cm$^2$. A complete analysis of data from tests that used very sensitive sensors will be conducted to determine the dark matter interactions involving $^6$Li. Such data will then be used to constrain dark matter interactions within different models and will be compared to the findings from other experiments.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, necessitating the use of additional constraints on the latent image. Our approach centers on the observation that natural images can be described as a combination of basic components or kernels, which serve as building blocks for reconstructing these images. By using the observed blurred image to estimate the distinct kernels and then applying them to a kernel-based reconstruction of the latent image, our method effectively performs blind image deblurring. This approach, which relies on alternating minimization to sequentially refine the images and its parameters, demonstrates exceptional results on synthetic datasets, surpassing notable benchmark methods, and also successfully handles challenging real-world deblurring scenarios, including motion artifacts, where other methods struggle.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-system. Furthermore, we establish an equivalence between Bihom-Yang-Baxter systems of weight λ and BiHom-Rota-Baxter systems of λ-duality. Lastly, we outline a method for constructing a wide range of BiHom-Yang-Baxter system solutions in this study.

Formal verification using Hoare logic has long been employed for establishing software correctness, yet contemporary software development demands more sophisticated correctness criteria.  The increasing intricacy of modern programs and systems, coupled with advanced functionalities such as data encryption and parallel processing, necessitate the ability to express correctness criteria across diverse domains.  Moreover, contemporary software engineering methodologies rely heavily on natural language for communication, necessitating the ability to translate natural language correctness criteria into a formal format for use with Hoare logic.  To address these challenges, we propose a formal framework that translates logical statements from a natural language subset into a format compatible with Hoare logic, and demonstrate its applicability by developing translators for logical constructs underlying the liveness specification language, SafetyCTL, and properties regarding parallel execution.  By leveraging our framework and related tools, developers can formally verify complex programs and systems, even those utilizing advanced features like parallel execution, from specifications expressed in natural language.

Distributed consensus is a fundamental concept that underpins various distributed systems. Canopus is a novel distributed consensus algorithm introduced in 2022 that achieves low latency and high availability. However, like most distributed consensus protocols, Canopus fails to prevent failures and susceptible to both benign and byzantine faults. RCanopus, the focus of this research, is a resilient consensus algorithm based on Canopus, integrating detection and handling mechanisms to ensure system resistance to failures. Firstly, RCanopus enhances non-terminative resistance through a failure detector, allowing the system to recover from multiple node failures. Secondly, a voting-based failure handler is implemented to address transient byzantine faults. Lastly, a upgraded Canopus consensus, OPC, has been incorporated into RCanopus to facilitate swift recovery during failure scenarios, with our simulation results demonstrating the system's superior performance in terms of latency compared to other existing resilient consensus algorithms.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo (NSE) and small-angle neutron scattering (SAS) have shown that lipid bending is suppressed in cholesterol-containing DOPC/DHPC mixtures, with specific bending modulus values identified. This finding challenges prior assumptions regarding SAS's ability to measure the bending modulus of lipid membranes, prompting a re-examination of its underlying assumptions. Our research reveals that undulations can significantly distort calculated bending modulus values, even at low wave numbers, necessitating their proper consideration in neutron scattering experiments.

This study develops and solves the Loop Quantum Gravity model of a universe filled with matter, specifically a scalar field at infinity, using the ADM Hamiltonian approach. By constructing the Hamiltonian and constraint operators, this research quantizes the model and obtains the quantum equations of motion. A comprehensive analysis of the quantum state of the universe's gravity and matter follows, revealing the scalar field's effects on the quantum model. A comparison with an otherwise identical model shows that in the classical limit, the two models yield identical results up to leading order in the quantum parameter but diverge at higher orders.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range between $5.1\times10^{19}$ eV and $1.6\times10^{20}$ eV. This
comprehensive dataset is being made available for researchers for further
investigation. A comprehensive error assessment is provided for each entry, 
including measurements of primary particle energy, arrival direction, and 
time. Additionally, the catalog's data is compared with recent findings from the 
Auger's third operational phase.

Incorporating uncertainty estimation into object detection is a critical component for developing more reliable and context-aware vision systems. Although recent advances in minimum entropy regression have shown promise, there remains a significant gap in the field regarding the accurate prediction of object localization uncertainty. This paper introduces BayesOD, a novel Bayesian approach designed for object detection uncertainty estimation. BayesOD is designed to be seamlessly integrated with existing object detection models, such as SSD300, without requiring any modifications to the model architecture or training process. Our results demonstrate that BayesOD produces more reliable uncertainty estimates and detection results in comparison to current state-of-the-art alternatives, as evidenced by lower negative log-likelihood scores and matching improved APd AP distance metrics.

The majority of existing traffic prediction models are created using city-wide traffic matrices, which are updated every few minutes and contain information about traffic on each road within a large area. This approach has a significant drawback: each matrix is composed of low-resolution fragments that provide little context about the continuous flow of traffic on individual roads. To overcome this limitation, we suggest a new paradigm that involves learning a full city-wide traffic matrix by analyzing just a small, representative snippet of each entry. Furthermore, we present a new time-series forecasting model specifically designed to utilize these traffic matrix snippets. Experimenting with these approaches on synthetic data and real-world datasets reveals that our snippet-based strategy can substantially enhance the interpretability of traffic prediction and also surpasses state-of-the-art performance.

In recent years, the concept of Gray monoids has resurfaced, with applications in various fields, including robotics, leading some researchers to suggest they are more robust than traditional monoids in addressing problems like the chaotic nature of information processing. Our paper delves into a systematic approach to define and rewrite Gray monoids. This involves creating a category equivalent to the category of all possible Gray monoids, which enables us to leverage the well-established techniques of rewriting theory. We also establish a coherence theorem for free monoids when viewed through the lens of Gray monoids. The implications of our work are twofold: it provides a unified framework for studying discrete time dynamical systems and automatically translates systems described using discrete monoids into discrete Gray monoids, effectively showcasing the versatility of our method.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on MRI scans is a critical component in diagnosing neurological disorders such as Alzheimer's disease and epilepsy. Current deep learning-based techniques for hippocampus segmentation rely heavily on single hippocampal subregion convolution, which may not be sufficient for distinguishing between distinct subregions. This paper presents a novel, multi-hippocampal subregion convolution network that improves hippocampal segmentation, particularly in cases of epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease. The network, called HipNet, consists of three distinct modules: (1) a multi-hippocampal subregion convolution network, (2) an adaptive module, and (3) a multi-scale feature aggregation module. The proposed HipNet architecture was evaluated on various public datasets and achieved superior segmentation results on the IBS challenge, as well as exceptional accuracy on epilepsy and Alzheimer's study scans.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties pass a single beam splitter with two paths each, while detecting only those particles that exit with a particular orientation. Our analysis, considering detection modes instead of spatial positions, reveals an apparent contradiction in the experimental findings, thus validating the exclusion principle's applicability in the experiment at hand.

Our research focuses on analyzing the behavior of cosmic ray antiprotons (CRAND) within low Earth orbits (LEO) using a Monte Carlo simulation. This study employs a Geant4-based simulation to trace particle movements, incorporating data from NASA's OMNI and GSFC models for solar modulation effects. In LEE, a significant increase in CRAND concentration occurs due to interactions with the Earth's Van Allen belts, resulting in antiproton levels exceeding 1 femtobarn ($10^{-15}$ per cm$^3$ per sr per eV) within certain 1 MeV energy ranges. We also investigate the potential impact of a space-based detector, such as the proposed COSI mission, on measuring CRAND distributions, utilizing magnetic field data from the NASA's OMNI and GSFC models.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
essential both for training and model selection. This work delves into a detailed 
analysis of the expressivity of global pyramid-like skeletonization in graph neural networks. 
We begin by proving its express limitations using a counterexample and establish its lower bound 
in terms of Lipschitz continuity. Furthermore, GCP-SNE's ability to effectively capture graph 
features is demonstrated through its performance on a variety of benchmark tasks. 
Building on this insight, we propose a novel approach to enhance local graph representation by 
reconfiguring the graph's structure, rather than relying on pre-defined pre-processing methods. 
Our novel edge linking technique significantly outperforms existing GNN-based methods on citation classification tasks.

To achieve differential privacy in low-rank matrix completion, this research introduces the first application of the truncated Huber loss mechanism, a robust loss function, to the problem. This is a significant extension of previous work on privately completing low-rank matrices, which has now been expanded to accommodate a broader class of differentially private output mechanisms, including the rounded Gaussian, and the truncated Huber loss mechanisms, among others.
