In an attempt to address this issue, we're exploring the use of unsupervised learning to establish a quantitative measure of the quality of synthetic entrainment. This involves defining a quality metric based on the assumption that matched speech patterns among human speakers serve as a reference for optimal performance. Our approach involves using pre-trained neural networks to extract and compare dynamic speech features from paired utterances, and in the process, we discovered that some features, like pitch, are more effective than others, like speech rate, at capturing finer distinctions in the model's performance.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are especially suited for processing
data from the RCsEd spectrograph, though these resources can be effectively utilized for
the analysis of data from similar spectrographs. Leveraging advanced web technologies
such as WebAssembly and Data-Parallel JavaScript, our tools enable swift data processing
on the client side without compromising performance. We've integrated visualization
capabilities into RCsEdv2, a RCsEd web-based data reduction pipeline, and also made
these visualization tools available as a standalone service for analyzing data from
spectrographs or any other dataset.

Most temporal action segmentation approaches rely on annotated boundary data.
However, we propose that everyday video experiences can effectively support the task of temporal action segmentation without supplementary annotations.
We introduce a novel, annotation-free framework called Self-supervised Co-occurrence Action Parsing (SSCAP) that capitalizes on human-generated video sequences for unsupervised temporal action segmentation.
We suggest that certain actions consistently occur together and utilize this assumption to develop a reliable means of accurately identifying action boundaries.
We achieve this by initially employing a self-supervised co-occurrence parsing approach to iteratively refine action boundaries based on relationships between adjacent actions.
Moreover, we incorporate two constraints: one that ensures actions within the same context share similar features, and another that enforces action boundary consistency.
We evaluate SSCAP on THUMOS14 and DAVIS datasets, demonstrating its superior performance over other supervision-free approaches, such as SUPREMACY, and S2VAE.

We've been using current algebra for nearly five decades to describe the properties of hadrons and their interactions, including quark currents and hadronic matrix elements. This method, rooted in QCD, relies on symmetries to derive relationships between different processes. The application of current algebra and the principles of the soft-collinear effective theory (SCET) has allowed us to accurately describe various five-quark hadronic states, particularly those involving charm and anti-charm quarks. The states $S_0$, $D_{s0}(2317)^{+}$, $D^{*+}K^{0}$, $J/\psi\pi$, $P_0^{5840}$, $D^+_{sJ}(2860)$, $J/\psi\pi$, $T_0^{5830}$, $D^+_{sJ}(2860)$, $J/\psi K$ and $P_S^{5870}$, $D^+_{sJ}(2860)$, $J/\psi K$ exhibit characteristics consistent with pentaquark states. The SCET framework has further enabled us to analyze these exotic states through the weak interactions of $B$ mesons, leading to the identification of novel form factors and theoretical predictions regarding weak decays.

Current educational tools primarily utilize two forms of feedback: traditional 
detailed feedback, which explains why answers are incorrect and how to improve, 
and inquiry-based feedback, which prompts students to analyze their understanding 
through in-depth questioning. Although inquiry-based feedback has been shown to be 
as effective as traditional feedback and promote better long-term learning and 
deeper conceptual knowledge, researchers have yet to explore its application in 
invariant inductive testing education. Our study investigates whether this 
approach can be effectively implemented in such a context by randomly assigning 
participants to receive either traditional detailed feedback or inquiry-based 
feedback on their testing strategies based on their responses.

Domain adaptation challenges arise in semi-supervised settings due to domain shifts between labeled source domains and partially labeled target domains. Traditional source-free domain adaptation methods, however, can mitigate domain shifts more effectively when source data is inaccessible. This work proposes a novel approach to enhance the classification performance of target domains in a partially supervised setting without access to source data. The method semi-supervised hypothesis transfer (SHT) transfers labeled and partially unlabeled high-performance hypotheses from multiple diverse domains to the target domain. Slightly adapting the transferred hypothesis through a fast fine-tuning process, SHT minimizes the effects of domain shifts and reduces the risk of incorrect hypothesis transfer. Experiment results demonstrate that SHT significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art source-free domain adaptation methods, with a substantial improvement of 10.4% in average accuracy.

A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems is conducted, focusing on their potential for deep space propulsion using gas-core reactor technology. The research includes developing detailed models of this system, which comprises a reactor, radiator, and engine components. By utilizing numerical methods, this power system is evaluated across a variety of design conditions to identify the optimal configuration that meets deep space propulsion requirements.

Identifying the precise 3D location of physical collisions is essential for detecting rare events in astroparticle physics, particularly when traditional tracking methods aren't applicable due to large detector volumes. We introduce a novel approach, called Domain-informed Neural Networks (DiNNs), specifically for localizing interaction points within large water Cherenkov detectors. Unlike standard CNNs, DiNNs incorporate a unique loss function that favors three-dimensional localization volumes within the detector's detection range. We test our method using simulation data, showing that DiNNs can learn locations of photon production more accurately than CNNs, with average localization errors of 17-21 cm compared to 25-31 cm for conventional models in water.

The development of direct imaging techniques for exoplanets has led to breakthroughs in characterizing planetary atmospheres beyond the atmospheric conditions of our Solar System. As interest in brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets continues to surge, particularly within cold environments, accurate model predictions become increasingly challenging due to the intricate nature of molecular absorption at low temperatures. Furthermore, the accurate detection of weak absorption signals necessitates access to a comprehensive database of absorption coefficients, especially for molecules such as NH3, H2O, and CH4, which are abundant in these planetary atmospheres. Unfortunately, such databases do not exist for brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheric conditions. In response to this gap, the EXOPLINES project has been initiated to address this critical need by developing an extensive database of absorption cross-sections for key molecules, spanning from 0.6 to 25 micrometers, incorporating data from quantum calculations, laboratory measurements, and astronomical observations.

This paper investigates the fundamental connection between answer sets and general logic programming (GELs), a more comprehensive extension of Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) that incorporates the possibility of contradictory theories. We show that the semantics of Answer Set Programming (ASP) can be understood through a constructive process that corresponds to a form of GEL. By redefining ASP's semantics as a form of GEL, we develop novel existence and uniqueness criteria for answer sets based on the principles of well-founded semantics and monotone inductive fixpoints. These new results build upon the existing well-founded semantics theory, offering both theoretical insights and potential computational benefits.

We have developed a novel resource theory applicable to all quantum states and operations to address fundamental questions about quantum operations and resource transformations in a generalized framework. By defining the amount of resource contained within an arbitrary quantum state or operation through a monotone function reliant on the relative entropy, we have established the first law of quantum theory, revealing that every fundamental property of the original resource is preserved within this generalized framework. We have found that the asymptotic convertibility principle holds true not just for a narrow subset of quantum operations but for a broader range of quantum operations as well. By extending our approach, we have demonstrated that the Pittenger-Halpern theorem can be generalized and serves as a multi-party extension of the Schmidt rank characterization, while also revealing a form of quantum state transformation asymptotic to a form of entanglement characterized by a rate. We have also examined properties of channels that remain invariant under free transformations, such as the quantum mutual information and quantum mutual coherence, and have found them superior to their traditional definitions. We have also discovered a form of asymptotic equivalence, known as asymptotic equivalence classes, which categorizes channels based on their free transformations and reveals an envariant property that asymptotic equivalence classes possess, thereby extending recent findings made by Verstraete, Vidal, and Cirac to the broader field of quantum theory.

To measure information from random variables in a universal way, we examine how one variable affects the knowability of another. This investigation involves exploring different information metrics as functions of a variable's moments. We find that in memoryless channels, certain components within these measures accurately capture signal power by directly representing the non-zero odd moments. Our research indicates that none of these information metrics can account for even moments without additional assumptions about the variables involved.

We develop a novel method for making probabilistic forecasts of future time series values based on past time series data, even in the absence of strict assumptions about time series behavior. Our approach relies on a smoothing lemma for high-dimensional normal distributions, which we use to create new statistical tests and estimators for dependence structures in multivariate time series. These new tools are specifically designed to handle heavy-tailed time series data without time series stationarity. We validate our method through numerical experiments using synthetic and real-world time series data, demonstrating its ability to outperform existing benchmarks in a wide range of scenarios.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs for LDPC codes suitable for quantum computing, enabling efficient decoding within linear time. The new code construction draws from classical LDPC codes based on finite geometries of a specific type. By adapting these patterns and leveraging innovations in proof technology, researchers can show that a significant subset of these codes, applicable in the quantum context, admits a strongly local check operator along with all other checks having high relative minimum weight in high-rate codes. As a result, these quantum codes can be decoded using sparse check-to-check and variable-to-check message passing, all in linear time. Furthermore, for any quantum LDPC code where every parity check can be considered as the sum of at least $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ independent parity checks, along with all other checks having high relative minimum weight, the developers can design a rapidly decodable, local, and quantum LDPC code family.

The distance $r$-dominating set problem, which is an approximation problem with high computational complexity for $r \geq 2$, becomes the standard dominating set problem when $r=1$. For large $r$, the problem becomes significantly more challenging to solve with good approximation ratios, particularly in dense graphs where the achieved ratio is poor. This paper focuses on improving the time complexity of distributed algorithms to solve the distance $r$-dominating set problem for specific graph classes within the LOCAL model. Achieving a distributed algorithm with a constant approximation ratio within the LOCAL model would be a significant advancement for graph classes. So far, a distributed algorithm with a constant approximation ratio for the distance $2$-dominating set has only been achieved for planar graphs in the global model. We propose a significant advancement in this field by constructing a distributed algorithm for constructing a distance $r$-dominating set on sparse high-girth graphs with $r \geq 2$. Our proposed algorithm is successful within the LOCAL model and can be implemented efficiently in specific graph classes, achieving a constant approximation ratio. We also present a significant advancement for high-girth graphs with a girth of $2k+1$, by constructing a distance $k$-dominating set with a constant approximation ratio within the LOCAL model.

This research examines how the correlation between topological properties and the relationships within bulk and boundary interfaces holds up in the presence of disorder in three-dimensional topological insulators with complex characteristics. Using numerical simulations, we investigate how specific boundary states respond to varying levels of disorder. Our analysis reveals that when a disorder level is present, certain boundary states become decoupled from both the bulk and gap regions, whereas others display an exponential reduction in overlap with the bulk as we move away from the surface. Interestingly, when we cut open the decoupled boundary states along horizontal or vertical axes, they split into pairs of states located at the intersections of the boundaries. These hinge states exhibit an overall overlap length, which is directly linked to the length of the hinge where the topological insulators are confined. Additionally, we explore the impact of varying disorder levels on the relationship between the bulk, boundaries, and hinge states.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the CMS experiment involve the decay of SUSY particles into the observable products of a Z boson and neutral Higgs particles of 95 fb^-1, collected from the 2016 and 2017 proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. These searches focus on three distinct supersymmetric models: a universal scalar and universal slepton model, a universal scalar and universal gaugino model, and the simplified model of a gluino-zeno-superparticle model. The first two models are analyzed through their missing energy and dijet/Z characteristics, while the third model is examined based on three distinct decay pathways based on the superparticle decay sequence. These analyses result in more stringent limits on supersymmetric mass parameters compared to previous studies utilizing simplified models.

We developed a series of linked projects aimed at creating digital avatars in the form of light field representations and multi-view video, allowing for seamless 3D interaction and seamless integration into various environments and 3D scenes. Our novel rendering technique combines these elements to 1) create and automatically adjust neural models of these and other 3D scenes and 2) generate high-quality, realistic multi-view videos from any possible angle without necessitating on-site capture. Building upon existing techniques, our model seamlessly integrates and surpasses current state-of-the-art algorithms, significantly enhancing our ability to create and manipulate complex 3D scenes.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020, involving SOAR/SPECKLE technology, yielded significant results. A total of 287 sessions were successfully completed, comprising 244 sessions utilizing K-band and 43 sessions employing J-band. Over 2800 images were taken, resulting in the acquisition of 188 binary and binary-like systems, along with the refinement of 10 existing orbits and the proposal of 10 new ones for further monitoring.

We are investigating chiral algebras found within celestial conformal field theory theories, specifically exploring them through the chiral algebras of 3D Yang-Mills theory and improved massless scalar multiplets as well as similar concepts in the improved De Rham and Maxwell theories. Chiral algebras associated with De Rham theory exhibit an infinite spin tower structure, where each component corresponds to the chiral algebra linked with an 3D free scalar field theory, revealing the ability of these theories to generate operator insertions with any integer or half-integer spin. We also explore the application of colour-kinematics duality in the context of chiral algebras, where we adapt dual-Kaneko duality from its original form in amplitudes and extend it to correlation functions, Chiral algebra operators, and OPEs. In particular, we extend the known colour-kinematics duality in the operator product expansion of primary operators within free conformal field theory to the chiral algebra setting. We establish the existence of kinematic factors in enhanced De Rham theory chiral algebras that satisfy the same algebraic relations found in enhanced Yang-Mills theory, where these factors are shown to be in one-to-one correspondence with the chiral algebra elements representing the commutators of primary operators within the chiral algebra setting.

A powerful and dynamic solar jet, known as AIA J1044, was studied using advanced imaging techniques and a low-frequency radio telescope. The analysis focused on a piston shock wave traveling along the jet axis, which exhibited complex behavior and distinct features in the image data. The study detected multiple piston shocks and estimated their speeds and temperatures at various locations. The analysis also revealed an extraordinary temperature of nearly 10 million Kelvin, far hotter than the sun's surface, and a connection between this shock and the jet's driving mechanism. The discovery provides valuable insights into the behavior of solar shocks and their role in energy release and heating.

A comprehensive likelihood analysis is performed on the general two Higgs doublet model in order to assess its capability in accommodating recent findings regarding flavour anomalies and particle physics measurements. The model under consideration allows for the presence of both Yukawa and Higgsino couplings. The $C^2$ statistic is defined in order to quantify the model's goodness-of-fit with the help of the $\chi^2$ function, which is constructed from the product of individual measurement probabilities. The model's parameters are then mapped out in the $M-2$ plane, which shows a preference for nearly degenerate Higgs masses and arbitrary Higgs coupling orientations, while excluding large top-Yukawa alignment angles. The model also cannot account for the $B$ physics anomalies simultaneously with $M_{H_2}^2 \gg M_W^2$. The model's predictions are then compared with recent Higgs coupling measurements.

This study introduces a unique, self-contained dynamic model for randomly distributed vortex systems in a two-dimensional space. Initially, we derive a finite vortex system equation in a specific probabilistic space, which, through an infinite limit, yields our proposed model for random vortex configurations in a broader, infinitely-dimensional space. We then establish essential properties for solutions to our derived equations, including a continuous and non-erratically shifting prospective framework. Ultimately, the created models effectively represent a new and coherent Gueniot process for randomly configured vortex systems.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using SQUID beam splitters and photodetectors. In this state vector, we identify and elucidate two types of entanglement: intermodal entanglement arising from the beam splayers and local entanglement occurring within detection events. We demonstrate that while the number of local entanglement events scales quadratically with the system size, we also show that intermodal entanglement only affects half the photons. As a means of quantifying these entanglement types, we propose using the minimum number of photons involved in each case.

Temporal sequence analysis has traditionally centered on shorter sequences, with the majority of approaches tailored for this purpose.  However, recent advancements in technology allow for the collection of much more detailed and rapid measurements, especially in the fields of life sciences and medicine. As a result, the analysis of temporal sequences has become increasingly challenging. A novel, data-driven method is proposed in this paper, leveraging neural networks to learn and match short sequences with longer ones. A training dataset is created using synthetic sequence pairs and applied to real-world measurements. Results indicate that a network trained on synthetic pairs is capable of effectively handling real-world sequences, even with high dimensions and length. Synthetic sequences provide a more accurate representation of the relationship between short and long sequences compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Reinforcement learning focuses on training agents to make the best decisions to gain the highest possible rewards in known environments. However, many real-world situations involve partial information and uncertain rewards, making it difficult for agents to make optimal decisions. Our research demonstrates that a specific type of neural network, the recurrent exponential family recurrent neural network (FERRN), can efficiently make optimal decisions even when agents have limited or incomplete information. We also show that the internal representations (beliefs) generated by FERRN in such unpredictable settings accurately reflect the current state of the environment, and we identify two primary strategies that these neural networks use to adapt to uncertain environments: one state-based approach and one factor-graph-based approach. Our findings not only explain how the human brain forms beliefs about uncertain environments but also reveal why certain types of recurrent neural networks are more effective than others in unpredictable settings.

In video action detection, current research often relies on classifying actions based on spatial and temporal features extracted from 2D or 3D convolutional networks.  However, we believe that understanding an action's context is crucial, especially since similar actions can occur in vastly different environments.  We've developed a novel graph-based approach that leverages context using either a pre-trained graph model or an individually constructed graph for each video, depending on availability.  We've also introduced a new loss function that enables the network to learn context independently of start/end predictions.  Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset for evaluating embedding quality in a controlled, synthetic setting with reduced challenges from data imperfections commonly found in real-world applications. Four prominent evaluation metrics were used in challenge, but it was discovered that common neural network training techniques, specifically network size and optimization methods, were more influential than embedding quality metrics. Despite significant innovations in the proposed embedding algorithms presented by the competitors, the established baseline, Virtuo, performed comparably. Consequently, the challenge objectives were successfully met, as the top submissions demonstrated substantial improvements in all three tasks using the four evaluation metrics.

This work explores stochastic differential equations that change over time and change slowly, particularly in cases where they become unstable when certain parameters reach specific values or levels. To achieve this, we're examining a broad category of parabolic partial differential equations with unstable coefficients for which precise calculations of solution errors are feasible, even in unstable areas. The solution involves utilizing nonlinear comparison techniques and the development of simplified models that gradually change. The research covers a range of topics, including topics of interest in both mathematics and physics, such as systems with multiple time scales, areas with changing characteristics, and the effects of stochastic perturbations on critical points and trajectories.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter in the context of the lochmann-coveney method (LOCV) within a strong, uniform magnetic field. The investigation particularly examines the effects of magnetic magnetic field on nuclear matter properties such as the energy per nucleon and the symmetry energy. Furthermore, the investigation has revealed that in the presence of a magnetic field, the incompressibility coefficient of nuclear matter significantly increases. As a result of enhanced number densities of particles and holes, the binding energy of $^{16}$O shows a greater magnitude in the presence of a magnetic field compared to its absence.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We develop a novel differential privacy mechanism based on gradient compression, which significantly reduces the rate of communication while still meeting the standards of differential privacy. This mechanism is integrated into a Federated Learning framework to create an optimized training algorithm. Theoretical analysis demonstrates the effectiveness of this algorithm, which we further substantiate through practical experiments.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet (FUV) study of the nearby Taurus-Perseus-Auriga complex revealed key insights into the star-forming region. Observations were made using the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Telescope (FUSE), which detected FUV emission from cosmic rays interacting with interstellar hydrogen in a 200 square degree survey area. By examining the 110-132 nanometer band, researchers measured the FUV emission and calculated the emission measure and ionization rate of the local interstellar medium. Results showed that the observed FUV emission could be attributed to cosmic rays ionizing neutral hydrogen, contradicting theories about photoionization by our galaxy's bulge. Data from both FUSE and the International Ultraviolet Explorer (IUE) revealed a correlation between FUV emission and radio continuum flux, which was found to be consistent with previous research. Unexpectedly, researchers discovered a significant discrepancy in FUSE data compared to IUE data, which was found to be statistically significant and warranted further investigation. Overall, researchers found that the observed properties of the local interstellar medium remained relatively stable over time, which was found to be consistent with previous research.

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information, making research accessible across numerous disciplines. However, extracting table data from PDFs remains a significant challenge due to the unformatted, raw structure within the documents. Traditional table extraction techniques often require manual input, making them time-consuming and prone to errors. Although recent deep learning-based approaches have been proposed, they still require manual structure creation, limiting their applicability. Our work capitalizes on the advancements in graph neural networks to develop a novel table extraction system that automatically identifies table structures within PDF documents, representing tables as graphs and nodes. The proposed system utilizes graph neural networks to learn a representation of the table structure, enabling it to capture the relationships between the table components. Experimental results on the InceptionDB dataset and human evaluations confirm the effectiveness of our method, as the proposed system's table structure representation accurately reflects the visual and semantic content of the tables, according to human evaluations.

This work delves into the dynamics of multi-stage games with uncertain outcomes, where sophisticated levels of reasoning influence strategies. Players, based on their known number of levels, strategize accordingly, assuming opposing players have lower level settings. In each game stage, players have the option to either withdraw or continue, with non-continuing players winning and others losing by not taking the winning action. Cautious players, however, employ indirect inferences to determine opponents' levels and respond with optimal K-level reasoning. We found that, in such settings, sustained progression through the game decreases as levels increase and strategic ambiguity arises regarding higher levels' existence.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions in developing countries. Our approach, which requires no survey data, leverages satellite imagery and pre-existing population data to provide and update population estimates in real-time. This method's accuracy is maintained by periodically updating with the latest census data when available. Our study focuses on enhancing population estimation in Mozambique by developing a model that divides the country into manageable grid cells and employs a deep neural network to predict population density. This network considers several features, including night-time light levels, land and water coverage, and historical population estimates, to make accurate predictions. Our results show that integrating night-time light data significantly improves prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that incorporating population data from the last census significantly enhances prediction accuracy over models that do not use this data. However, our research highlights the need for continued evaluation of model performance in areas affected by significant urban development, such as the rapidly growing city of Beira, where previous models struggled to make accurate predictions due to unexpected changes in population density.

Over the past ten years, researchers have extensively studied the ability to efficiently identify items within a dataset, specifically by minimizing memory usage and providing a guaranteed not-missed item query outcome. This approximate membership query issue, specifically the fully-passive counterpart, has garnered significant interest. This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach to tackle this query challenge by combining multiple distinct hash sets in tandem, providing an almost guaranteed not-missed item query outcome with significantly reduced false positives compared to using a solitary hash set, specifically by approximating $O(\frac{\log_{b} N + \log_{b} \epsilon}{p})$ space requirements where $N$ is total memory usage, $p$ is maximum possible query outcome probability of failing to detect an item, and $\epsilon$ is maximum possible false positive probability. Furthermore, this work demonstrates practical applicability of this concept in developing compact representations of data with near-zero false positives by combining hash-based data structures with zlib compression methods to create efficient representations of dictionaries and other large datasets.

We have designed an experiment to convert from atoms to dimers and then to molecules through three-body recombination, aiming to develop a highly stable quantum source of polar molecules based on fermions. In a magnetic field-free environment, we'll use a highly efficient process that leverages the spin-exchange interaction between atoms at around 500 nanoKelvin to capture unstable clusters. Our research indicates a potential production rate of 10 to 15 million dimers per second, given that we have 100,000 spin-exchange collisions occurring every second in our experiment, relying solely on a laser beam for creation without needing a sympathetic cooling process. Our approach can also be adapted for other atomic and elemental systems where Fano-Feshbach resonances cannot be utilized.

In this research, we introduce a novel multi-resolution Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) method designed to simulate complex multi-phase fluid structure interactions. This approach capitalizes on the interactions between a high-resolution boundary layer and a coarse outer flow to efficiently capture relevant details. To achieve this, we employ two multi-resolution solvers, one for the free surface phase and one for closed phases, utilizing the former as a boundary for the latter. Our SPH method is built upon an earlier multi-resolution framework developed by our group, adapting it for phases with no-flow boundaries. This allows for the simulation of fluids falling or flowing past solid objects. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through a series of tests, particularly with a droplet descending under gravity. The predicted terminal velocity of the droplet is compared with that of a lower-resolution simulation and with other published studies. Furthermore, we apply our method to a variety of scenarios, including multi-phase BSIs with different types of objects and with or without circulation.

Recent advancements in near-term quantum devices necessitate the development of both quantum-supervised and quantum-unsupervised learning algorithms. To address this need, a pair of machine learning algorithms based on stochastic quantum circuits have been developed, with designs that cater to the near-term quantum hardware landscape. Specifically, a quantum-unsupervised learning algorithm and a quantum-supervised model were created, with the latter's model reusing its circuit for evaluation to minimize gate depth. Furthermore, its architecture features parameter reuse and entanglement, making it adaptable for various problems and comparable to classical neural networks in near-term quantum hardware. To demonstrate the quantum algorithms, experimental results on the development of quantum classifiers and a pattern clustering approach have been achieved using their corresponding quantum circuits. These findings, with results in evaluation metrics, were obtained after running the algorithms on a superconducting quantum processor with 5 qubits.

A recent technique called FastPitch allows users to control pitch in speech by providing pitch contours as a reference. However, it has been discovered that FastPitch is not very effective at producing accurate speech when the pitch varies with a fixed rate. Our solution, called Pitch Augmentation (PiAu), can improve this shortcoming. PiAu does this by automatically increasing the rate of the reference pitch contour while maintaining the overall pitch pattern and the speaker's unique voice characteristics. We used the SI-SALTI speaker to test PiAu by comparing the pitch control of the modified system and the original FastPitch system at various pitch rates and speakers. Our results show that PiAu can significantly improve the effectiveness of the FastPitch model at high pitch rates.

This research focuses on solving spatio-temporal reasoning problems through sequence prediction, using scene descriptions and spatial relationships as input. While previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of the Transformer architecture, they primarily concentrated on single-hop prediction tasks. In contrast, we tackled the more complex task of predicting the location of objects across multiple hops in a scene and achieved this by employing a novel, efficient approach inspired by graph neural networks, without relying on an explicit graph structure. Our method, named Hopper, demonstrated superior performance on two popular datasets: CLEVR and APERA.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production accompanied by a bottom quark pair at the Large Hadron Collider. The process is explored through modified vector-like top and bottom quark analogues, known as $B^*-3/2$ and $T^0$, respectively. The investigation utilizes the CMS experiment's data on $W$ boson production paired with bottom quarks, covering a range of invariant masses from 45 to 115 GeV. The data analysis is carried out with 19.7 inverse femtobarns of integrated luminosity from 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. The results of the analysis have led to a precise measurement of $W$ boson mass, with the outcome of 80.34 GeV, having a statistical error of 0.12 GeV and a systematic error of 0.04 GeV. The study has also found no observable signs of $W$ boson production beyond 115 GeV. The findings are in line with the predictions of the Standard Model, yet there has been a noticeable, small deficit in data that might be explained by an unaccounted-for background from $Zc(3873)$ particles.

Remote-controlled robots are becoming increasingly useful in various applications such as education, security, and the service industry. Their potential is hindered by control difficulties stemming from latency, inaccuracy, and other issues that impact user experience quality. To address this problem, this study focuses on developing an efficient quality of experience assessment method for these robots that is grounded in psychology. By analyzing a user's experience through a human-centric approach, this method evaluates how well a user can perform their task, how they perceive the control quality, and how they emotionally react to the process. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this assessment method, it is applied to a telepresence robot control scenario and compared with traditional methods. The results indicate that this method provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the user's experience and can effectively identify and rectify control inaccuracies.

In this study, we revisit the core features of two Bayesian hierarchical regression models, thoroughly analyzing their full probabilistic framework and incorporating the Gompertz and logistic residual distributions to better fit data. We thoroughly examine the derivation and implementation of Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, along with the findings from experiments conducted using synthetic data and the voice pitch dataset.

In this model, we analyze the game of Mafia by breaking it down into distinct phases. Within each phase, Mafia players collaborate to make decisions that benefit their team, followed by a similar process for civilians. Our model considers the implications of players leaving the game, with Mafia players targeting the civilians who pose the greatest threat to their team's success. A mathematical model is developed to quantify the probabilities of various outcomes in the first two phases of the game. Our analysis indicates a clear mafia advantage in the first phase and a closely contested situation in the second phase.

Planet formation is a complex process that involves several mechanisms, including core accretion and gravitational instability. Planets with a mass exceeding 10 Jupiter masses are believed to form through core accretion, while those with a mass less than this threshold are thought to develop through gravitational instability. We conducted a series of 3D simulations to better understand the simultaneous growth of two massive planets and their impact on the formation of a protoplanetary disk. Our high-resolution simulations, based on the GLM-GLAM code, explored how two massive planets interact with their surroundings and grow over time. We found that massive planets can cause significant changes to the gas around them, creating a void and further altering the environment. These findings suggest a possible explanation for observed phenomena in binary star systems, such as lower disk masses at large distances from the central star compared to single stars. Additionally, our results indicate that massive planets can limit the amount of gas available for the growth of nearby smaller planets, potentially affecting their final mass.

The electronic transport properties in thin films composed of silicon-doped armchair carbon nanotubes, measured at 10 Kelvin with high electrical field intensities exceeding 1 Volt per nanometer, have been investigated. A previously reported non-linear relationship between the current and applied voltage in these films, observed under such conditions, has now been experimentally confirmed. Utilizing detailed simulations, the temperature-dependent non-linearity was found to be a direct result of a specific interaction involving phonons and electrons, occurring between parallel tubes within the film. Notably, this temperature-dependent behavior was also observed when electron transport was affected by intertube interactions rather than intratube phenomena.

This research introduces a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is built upon entropy, which enables dimension reduction and assigns weights to data points in high dimensional space based on their weights. The dimensionality is effectively reduced and data is grouped into subspaces with varying entropy levels. The method is tested on three cluster human genome datasets to compare its performance with existing state-of-the-art algorithms in terms of clustering accuracy and computational efficiency. The results show that our proposed algorithm consistently surpasses the benchmark methods in all tested scenarios.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been widely used in practice, yet theoretical research on their consistency has remained largely unresolved. Our study investigates the properties of two distinct MOE algorithms. The first algorithm employs an online approach with independent and identically distributed data, demonstrating that under general conditions, at least one expert for each data subset must be activated. The second algorithm examines the potential of applying proximal methods to the stochastic setting, showing that a modified version of this method can consistently estimate MOE parameters when the sample size increases. The updated algorithm reveals a numerical advantage by reducing a previously identified difficulty with non-identical data. Our theoretical findings are supported by simulation results.

This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs and its connection to Jacobians and Prym varieties, originally used in the context of the octagon curve family. Initially developed as teaching material for UC Berkeley's Introduction to Riemann Surfaces course during the spring of 2021, these notes were subsequently revised for clarity.

While not yet measured with certainty, a predominantly non-zero cosmic birefringence angle, in many instances around 10 degrees, has been reported from recent B-mode polarization data. Such a result would strongly imply a beyond-Standard-Model presence in the early universe, possibly even a gravitational influence from any global symmetries that break at the quantum level. If these findings are verified, they could significantly narrow down the theories explaining inflation and point towards solutions for the muon g-2 anomaly.

Our research centers around the globular cluster NGC 4147, where we've obtained wide field of view spectra of its brightest stars using a French telescope's UVIT instrument. These stars were selected based on their optical magnitudes and subsequently categorized as blue horizontal branch stars, red horizontal branch stars, giants, and sub-giants. These classifications were refined using artificial neural networks. Subsequent spectral analysis yielded detailed measurements of effective temperatures, surface gravities, and surface abundances of hydrogen, helium, oxygen, carbon, calcium, and iron. Our research indicates that blue horizontal branch stars exhibit consistent characteristics with red horizontal branch stars, whereas blue horizontal branch stars possess unique surface abundances of calcium and oxygen. Moreover, we've discovered a correlation between oxygen abundance and distance from the cluster center but not with other chemical elements.

This note presents a new category of topological spaces, denoted as CWC, which is more restrictive than the existing class of spaces with CW properties. Within the class CWC, we demonstrate that the functor mapping homotopy types to maximal graphs of a space I(X) has an inverse. Consequently, this result enables the establishment of a CWC space X's homotopy type based on its M(X) and the related mapping cones formed in the sieve of X's maximal graph. Furthermore, we show that the functor mapping the homotopy type of X's nth mapping cone to I(X)'s maximal graphs has an inverse, which is consistent with the findings of the M. Miller and D. Mumford conjecture for moduli spaces of curves.

The goal of deep transferability research is to identify what characteristics in a neural network allow it to generalize effectively to unseen domains. Two significant consensus views currently prevail in the field, however, our analysis contradicts both. Firstly, despite the consensus that generalizable distributions should share underlying concepts, our research reveals that novel distributions may actually contain novel data points. Secondly, the prevailing assumption that network parameters alone account for generalizable behavior is refuted by our findings, which suggest that other factors, including the data distribution, also play a role. Through experiments involving image classification and generative models, our results demonstrate that our proposed theory aligns well with observed generalizable performance.

In various systems, from ecosystems to social networks, the structure plays a critical role in information diffusion. Specifically, networks with high and low clustering coefficients exhibit distinct diffusion characteristics, with information spreading more efficiently in networks with randomly distributed connections compared to locally clustered networks. Notably, in networks where hubs are well-connected, local clusters may actually impede information diffusion. This phenomenon challenges conventional wisdom and suggests that understanding information diffusion in complex networks requires considering the interplay between network structure, information, and the global hub nodes.

For any simple curve in the projective plane, we weaver an ideal line arrangement in an expanded space that includes curves exhibiting the maximum possible multiplicity interactions. We derive precise lower bounds for specific values that measure how the line orientations differ, specifically values known as the $\delta$ invariants, which depend solely on the curve's complexity and topological properties. These new bounds significantly surpass older results in their tightness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these properties hold for curves with specific complexities and topological properties. Additionally, we prove that a particular type of measurement related to the phase alignment of the curve's components remains strictly positive for curves with sufficient complexity.

The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard approach for perturbation analysis was investigated for cases without amplification. The findings show that although this model provides a convenient linear approximation for signal propagation, it results in a significant increase in relative error when the time step size is increased, limiting its practical utility.

The widespread adoption of Android devices among the general population has made them vulnerable to malware, which poses a significant threat to user and system security. Android's openness and extensive user base have enabled the creation of numerous and sophisticated malware variants within a short period. One approach to evading anti-malware detection involves concealing malicious code, utilizing social engineering, or masking malicious intent. Recently, the emergence of problem-space evasion attacks has presented a groundbreaking technique for avoiding detection, utilizing unique and novel features of Android to bypass security checks. These attacks leverage user-generated content such as SMS, contacts, and camera data to disguise themselves as legitimate apps. To date, the application of problem-space evasion attacks in the Android ecosystem remains understudied. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of this emerging threat, offering an in-depth examination of existing research and identifying several unresolved challenges.

Service-oriented computing utilizes services as a method to execute business processes, where each service is a collection of related tasks, services, and data that work together to achieve a common goal. A service's functionality is represented through its operations and the data exchanged with other services. As services are designed to be independent, they can be developed by separate teams and even located on separate systems, with their interactions based on agreed-upon interaction protocols.

A service's internal workings are based on its underlying workflow. The structure of a service can be represented as a directed graph, with nodes representing sub-services and task units, and edges representing data flow and dependencies. To manage complex services and interconnections, it's essential to have a standardized way of representing and coordinating these units.

This paper introduces Ozy, a new service orchestration container, which provides a common framework for representing service units and their underlying workflow structures. The Ozy container aims to overcome challenges associated with service representation and interconnections by offering a standardized way of organizing service units, while minimizing the impact on interconnections by not including task units that transfer services between domains.

Recent experiments involving high-moblicity silicon-based quantum wells have revealed an unexpected re-entrant half-quantum Hall phase characterized by a quantum Hall conductivity of 5/2, suggested to be related to a neutral excitation as predicted by the Moore-Read phase theory. Contrary to previous studies that linked the phenomenon to a particle-hole symmetric triplet state at strong Landau level mixing, our comprehensive investigation based on a boson Monte Carlo theory suggests the occurrence at moderate level mixing under strong magnetic fields and weak interparticle interactions. Notably, our results reveal the phase persists under broken particle-hole symmetry near the strong level, thereby challenging the previous hypothesis.

Our analysis reveals that the conditions for forming stable objects with cosmic-scale masses and extremely low temperatures are identical to those for forming binary black holes through a Thakurta-like collision. However, using the Thakurta metric to describe the low-temperature equilibrium state of such objects is flawed. In reality, the conditions for creating low-temperature objects with large masses are extremely restrictive, and their production is severely limited by various processes. Consequently, these objects are unlikely to exist and, even if they did, would be almost entirely absent. LIGO-Virgo's constraints on cosmic black holes remain valid.

The standard explanation for pebble accretion involves a gas of solid particles under hydrostatic equilibrium, which forms a pebble gas that can significantly impact planet formation.  However, this model may be altered if dynamic effects, such as fluid instabilities, cause significant gas velocity fluctuations that exceed the escape velocity of a growing planetary body.  To investigate this possibility, we simulated planet formation using 3-dimensional planet formation models and found that fluid instabilities can lead to the formation of pebble rings and trails around protoplanets.  The pebble rings can persist for a considerable amount of time and can be influenced by density fluctuations in the gas.  This study demonstrates that a simpler 2-dimensional model may be inadequate in representing planet formation and that 3-dimensional simulations are necessary to accurately model this process.

When solving linear regression, we often find that a vast number of different hypothesis functions can lead to the same optimal result under the condition that each achieves a perfect fit for the given data points and noise. Nonetheless, we consider a more realistic scenario where the matrix representing hypothesis parameters has specific, restricted structures rather than being any arbitrary configuration. By examining under what conditions such restricted matrices have a reduced number of optimal results, even with perfect data fit, we demonstrate that a large abundance of different hypothesis parameters exists. Specifically, given that the matrix represents an orthogonal polynomial basis, nearly all parameters exist for cases where the number of data points significantly exceeds the degree of the polynomial. This parameter diversity exists within the space of all possible matrices rather than being confined to a specific optimal result. The implications of this phenomenon are that under conditions where a large abundance of parameters exist, overparameterization effects remain present even when utilizing regularization and achieving a perfect fit for data points.

We prove that in any countable abelian group, a large enough Bohr set's subgroup has a bounded index. This implies a significant result: in a group that doesn't have significant structure, the sum of two sets avoiding periods results in a set that's significantly non-symmetric under with respect to at least one period. As a consequence, a recent multilinear Fourier transform estimate for groups without significant structure can be derived, which in turn leads to an improvement of a theorem relating to the sumset of sets in groups without significant structure.

This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban centers, where traditional methods of door-to-door transportation collections prove inefficient due to severe traffic congestion. To overcome this challenge, we propose a two-stage solution approach that first determines an optimal turn-point for each customer request, and then generates efficient routes considering traffic conditions, as well as other standard constraints. Given the complexity of traffic conditions, we rely on a mathematical programming model incorporating additional parameters, and use a branch-and-cut algorithm to find near-optimal route solutions that account for traffic conditions.

This study explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for product data in E-commerce settings, addressing the challenge of extracting meaningful features from diverse sources such as images and titles. Our approach, based on contrastive learning, accounts for both direct and indirect connections between modalities. Through pretraining, it can capture richer features for E-commerce applications like search relevance and understanding. To assess its performance, we created a comprehensive product multi-modal dataset called E-commerce-MMLU, which includes a wide range of images and titles from diverse categories. Results indicate that our proposed pretraining method outperforms existing benchmarks, especially in E-commerce search tasks. Additionally, our findings show that our approach leads to notable improvements of up to 9.8% in accuracy for the actual search task.

A significant challenge in non-invasive conversion therapy research is the curse of dimensionality caused by the intricate dependencies within neuroimaging data. This limitation has restricted the effectiveness of dimensionality reduction techniques, such as autoencoders, in neural network-based conversion therapy. To address this issue, we introduce a novel information-based neural network framework, called Deep InfoMax, which directly minimizes the mutual information between latent variables, thereby learning rich representations of data. By leveraging this capability, we demonstrate the ability to effectively capture latent cognitive states from various neuroimaging modalities, thereby accurately predicting whether a given subject will convert to a higher disease stage. Our results show that using multiple imaging modalities yields superior accuracy compared to using a single modality. Additionally, we employ t-SNE visualization to uncover hidden patterns within the data, thereby providing valuable insights into the effectiveness of our neural representation learning approach.

One significant challenge in natural language processing lies in accurately interpreting linguistic meanings. Building on Caput et al.'s work on neural networks with interaction-based semantics, this research extends capacity by employing recurrent neural networks and adding word-order interpretation through an attention mechanism. Additionally, an optimization technique known as ORB has been incorporated, allowing the model to consider all linguistic meanings equally without prioritizing one over another. The results from these advancements have been systematically evaluated using a comprehensive benchmark consisting of three datasets, each testing different levels of semantic understanding, from basic to complex.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital model by using numerical methods based on self-consistent DMFT. An on-site Coulomb interaction is employed rather than explicit spin-orbit basis with off-diagonal coupling. The goal is to identify conditions where interactions surpass spin-orbit coupling effects in quantum fluctuations near the metal-insulator phase boundary. A key approach involves monitoring the temperature dependence of magnetic fluctuations as the system moves from insulating to metallic states. Our findings suggest that a specific type of magnetic symmetry, quadrupolar, along with a multi-orbital setup, facilitates the enhancement of spin-orbit coupling over interactions when the system approaches the metal-insulator phase boundary.

A metastable dark matter candidate with a  0.1 - 1 TeV mass,  10^10 - 10^12 seconds lifetime, and a  10^-6 GeV decay rate, leads to observable consequences such as dark matter decay, gamma ray emission, and disruption of dark matter halos. This uniform decay of dark matter produces sigmas of  10^-5 - 10^-4, consistent with Planck data, although it is in tension with Fermi-LAT observations of dark matter halos. Furthermore, this uniform decay leads to significant disruption of dwarf galaxies, causing mass loss of  10-30% and a reduction of sigma by factor of 2-3, consistent with observations of the Milky Way and the detection of white dwarfs with dark matter decaying. Moreover, the uniform decay of dark matter is uniform across all scales, predicting a correlation between the mass of Milky Way satellite galaxies and their internal velocity dispersions.

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices function effectively even in unforeseen circumstances, we need to develop more robust evaluation techniques to simulate unpredictable testing conditions.  This requires novel metrics that capture AI behavior in environments that differ from those used for training.  This paper proposes using nonparametric, distribution-free prediction intervals to create such metrics, which come with theoretical guarantees of accuracy.  It also presents a new approach, the distribution shift adjusted TPI, to improve these predictions under real-world distribution shifts.  By leveraging conformal prediction, these adjusted predictions come with confidence intervals, allowing us to assess AI performance across various clinical tasks.  This study evaluates the performance of these prediction intervals and a standard metric across AI models, with a particular focus on AI models applied to pulse oximetry, an application where inaccurate predictions can lead to serious consequences.  Experimental results show that our adjusted prediction interval achieves better performance, with significantly narrower intervals and improved accuracy.

While molecular dynamics simulations are a cornerstone of modern biomolecular research, their utility is often limited by computational constraints and short timescales. Recent advancements in enhanced sampling methods have effectively addressed these limitations, making DNA structure analysis a prominent application area. We introduce the rigid base biasing (RBB) algorithm, designed to expedite the dynamic simulation of double-stranded DNA. By incorporating controlled, collective movements of base pairs, the RBB algorithm enhances the sampling efficiency of DNA conformations. Leveraging the metadynamics approach, our study explores various ways to implement and optimize the RBB algorithm for various DNA sampling challenges. We identify a prominent feature in DNA sampling - the considerable contribution of base pair rigidity - and propose strategies to improve its detection and quantification, ultimately facilitating more effective DNA conformations sampling.

In 2005, Alon Drucker introduced the Adaptive Number System, an innovative entropy encoding technique surpassing traditional techniques like Huffman coding, arithmetic encoding, and LZMA. Drucker proposed a method of entropic compression using e^2 approx 7.389, but with uncertain actual performance. Our research provides the first comprehensive evaluation of ANS compression capabilities. We demonstrate that an optimal version of ANS can reach the theoretical minimum compression threshold, while current implementations can only achieve this goal partially. A partial analysis of the algorithm's actual compression efficiency was previously presented by Ross and Grossfield. Our findings show that a full analytical evaluation had been theoretically possible, with the main remaining challenge being the mathematical complexity. Our work further identifies and resolves specific implementation challenges that prevent real-world applications from reaching their theoretical potential.

The dielectric characteristics of micro- and mesoporous materials heavily rely on  water in their microstructure pores.  In our study, we employ dielectric  spectroscopy to investigate pore solution behavior and its interaction with  pore surfaces in a wide frequency range between 1 and 100 MHz.  Using an  equivalent circuit model, we model electrolyte-pore system responses and  identify  the pivotal  physical processes governing pore solution  electro-dynamics.  Moreover, we  apply surface conductivity theory to determine surface charge density and its  spatial distribution within pores.  Ultimately, our findings can inform the  development of high-sensitivity electrical sensors for monitoring the curing and  hardening processes of cement-based materials.

In our earlier work, we successfully used the Bethe-Salpeter equation with the one-boson-exchange potential to derive the hadron-heavy hadron hadronic molecules, including $X(3872)$ and a number of additional states. Our current research delves into the heavy-heavy hadronic molecule diquark-antidiquark states in the D-Dbar and charmonium-D or Psi'-Dbar channels by applying the same framework used in our previous studies. Furthermore, we investigate the potential for the formation of the hidden heavy-heavy tetraquarticle state, utilizing the predicted resonance from the recent LHCb findings, namely a $\Xi'_c^{-}$ and its antiparticle the $\Xi'_c^+$. Our analysis also explores a number of decay modes for the detected resonance $\Xi'_c^+$. The primary focus of our research is to determine the mass of the $\Xi'_c^+$, which is expected to reside within the $\Xi'_c(2468)D$ or $\Xi'_c(2468)\bar D$ threshold. Our results reveal a narrow resonance at $5.90$ MeV below the $\Xi'_c(2468)D$ or $\Xi'_c(2468)\bar D$ threshold along with the $\Xi'_c(2468)\Psi'(1S)c$ threshold. Our research also provides predictions for the

We conduct a direct cosmological inference from the correlation functions of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, using a novel statistical method that bypasses the conventional approach of comparing pixelated spectra. Through a precise measurement of the baryon acoustic oscillation peak from the quasar SDSS-DR16, our cross-correlation analysis reveals the most accurate and model-independent constraints on cosmological parameters. The results show a precise measurement of the distance redshift curve at low redshifts, with an inferred $(d_c/z)_{1{\rm dex}}$ of $6412\pm 84$ Mpc, in agreement with the $\Lambda$CDM model but deviating from the DC$\Lambda$ model. Furthermore, our research establishes a significant tension between the local Hubble constant measurements and the $\Lambda$CDM model, with $1\sigma$ agreement for the $\sigma_8$ parameter but disagreement for the optical depth parameter $\tau_{\rm eff}$, given the Planck+R16 values.

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully demonstrated a novel beam manipulation process, known as emittance exchange, in a fast-cycling cyclotron operating at 250 MeV/u. A carefully arranged set of quadrupole magnets, synchronized with the beam's orbital motion, exchanges the horizontal and vertical axes, effectively swapping the characteristics of the two planes. This technique can serve as a means to stabilize beams by combining a plane with a stable dynamic aperture with a plane featuring a lower density of unstable orbitals. Additionally, this beam configuration can facilitate the development of stable, small-emittance beams, crucial for applications in fixed-target experiments, ion implantation, and thin foil stripping.

A fundamental task in traffic safety and prediction, as well as a crucial aspect of artificial intelligence, is modeling human behavior. To predict traffic behavior, the most effective approach is to create a model that represents traffic patterns. The most widely used technique involves dividing a trajectory into segments and predicting each segment sequentially. However, this method has a significant drawback: the predicted information can be inaccurate, leading to subpar predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce a sequential cross-attention mechanism. This mechanism allows the model to condition each segment prediction on all available trajectory information, rather than just the previous frame. Furthermore, we incorporate a moving window that gradually updates the trajectory encoder's information, making the model more efficient. The proposed model, Social-aware Trajectory Prediction (TRIP), achieves significant improvements. Experimental results demonstrate that TRIP surpasses state-of-the-art methods by 10% in AUC-DE and 8% in AUC-100 metrics, while requiring less than 50% additional parameters and a minimal increase in computation.

Over the past few decades, various theoretical models have been introduced to analyze machine learning systems, with the aim of understanding their inherent properties. This study compares two distinct entropy models, the information theoretic measure of complexity (IMEC) and the generalized Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy (GKSE), to assess their effectiveness in characterizing Boltzmann machines. The GKSE, an extension of Shannon's entropy rate, has previously been applied in neural modeling, but its limitations are apparent when used to characterize Boltzmann machines. In contrast, the IMEC concept has shown greater utility in characterizing similar systems. Through numerical experiments, we evaluate the performance of both entropy measures on Boltzmann machines, revealing that the GKSE is suboptimal, while the IMEC yields more accurate results. Additionally, we highlight that these entropy measures are not interchangeable, but rather each possesses unique capabilities.

This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves identifying hand gestures to steer autonomous robots. To achieve this, we have developed a decentralized gesture recognition system that relies on either long short-term memory networks or bidirectional long short-term memory networks. Our experiments were conducted using a dataset containing hand gesture signals simulated by a virtual human hand. To test the technique in a more practical setting, we collected real hand signals and used a decentralized gesture recognition system to control a swarm of six autonomous mobile robots. Our results, obtained through both simulated and actual experiments, indicate that the technique can be effectively applied to a range of applications, including swarm robotics and augmented virtual environments.

The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment.

A key advantage of counterdiabatic driving is its capacity to force a system to follow the changing ground state of a target Hamiltonian when the parameter is adjusted over time. Unfortunately, implementing this approach often requires detailed knowledge of the Hamiltonian's level structure. In this paper, we demonstrate that a simplified model of a system, which only requires an estimate of the ground state overlap can be used to effectively prepare the ground state via a two-stage process. First, a coarse model is used to control ground-state preparation. Then, a fine-tuned version of the Hamiltonian, with its ground state closely resembling that of the original system, is used to fine-tune the prepared state using a new method that doesn't involve time derivatives. In practice, we apply a combination of this approach with the projected variational method to find a suitable ground-state-like expression for the Hubbard model, showing through the comparison of the final states that the combined approach is as effective as using the fine-tuned Hamiltonian alone.

Color consistency is a crucial factor in computer vision applications, where decolorization methods are employed to prepare images for tasks such as object recognition. This research presents an innovative and data-driven method for removing coloration in images, which is an essential step in tone-mapping applications. The proposed technique has been found to significantly expedite the decolorization process compared to conventional methods, while also maintaining color homogeneity across images. The speed advantage stems from a simplified calculation approach, which bypasses complex computations. The effectiveness of the proposed method was substantiated through comparisons with established decolorization techniques, including the adapted-Color Similarity Method and the color negation method, which yielded comparable results in terms of color homogeneity. The proposed technique exhibited an average processing time of 0.00066 seconds per image, underscoring its speed advantage over traditional methods, which typically take 0.0296 seconds or more.

This research develops an expression to decompose infinitely differentiable complex-valued functions into a sum of exponentials along with a corresponding error term. Building upon this, it demonstrates the convergence of a corresponding infinite series and reveals that it accurately represents all smooth functions on the real number line. A key advantage of this series over its traditional polynomial counterpart, the Taylor series, lies in its capacity to avoid a circular definition when employed within problem-solving contexts, particularly in a multidisciplinary field such as mathematical physics, reliant on smooth, function-based problem-solving.

Given a surface S equipped with a metric d, such that it is topologically equivalent to a disk and satisfies the CAT(0) condition, we will demonstrate the existence of a non-constant harmonic function u from S to the complex plane, such that its pullback metric is bounded from below with a Riemannian metric. Furthermore, if S also has a length space property, we will prove the existence of a harmonic branched covering p from S to a surface X, where X possesses a singular conformal structure and is topologically equivalent to a disk. Notably, X will be shown to carry a singular CAT(0) metric and admit a conformal singular CAT(0) structure that is conformally equivalent to a smooth CAT(0) metric. This result generalizes previous findings by Ahlfors, whose theorem on the uniformization of the complex plane involved a bounded conformal metric and a bounded holomorphic function, rather than a CAT(0) surface and a harmonic function.

Low-energy photon-photon scattering, a theory verified by both quantum electrodynamics and experimental findings, can now be studied in detail thanks to new laser technology. This breakthrough is made possible by combining advanced laser systems with plasma systems, which allow for a thorough examination of the theory in an extremely intense environment. This intense setting can be achieved in just a few femtoseconds using quantum electrodynamics corrections, which could lead to significant advancements in physics research.

We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-covered' and found both these shape-based dependencies and the linear temporal shape constraints to be expressible through first-order logic formulas.

A new package called pyStoNED has been developed to provide a Python interface for simultaneous quantile efficient distance regression, allowing users to obtain an alternative measure of technology efficiency under heterogeneous production conditions. The package includes a method for estimating the minimum cost of inputs required to achieve a specific level of output at any given quantile of the technology frontier. In situations where a direct estimate of the general production function may not be feasible due to a large number of inputs, the package also provides a way to estimate a local version of this function using a nonparametric approach based on input and output observations that share similar characteristics.

This paper outlines a search for light Higgs bosons using top-quark pairs produced in single and double Higgs-associated events at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). The search targets the production of a top-quark pair accompanied by a Higgs boson, either a 125 GeV Higgs or a lighter variant, in proton-proton collisions at an energy of 13 TeV with a data set of 137 inverse femtobarns. The study considers Higgs decays into a photon and a W boson, or two photons, and employs a variety of search strategies to isolate signal from background, including a four-lepton search, a three-lepton search, and a two-lepton search, all accompanied by a significant transverse momentum. The application of a b-tagging technique and a series of cuts on the invariant mass of the final state particles enable the identification of distinct search channels, such as the four-lepton search, and are further refined using multivariate analysis methods, including boosted decision trees. The results of the study demonstrate a significant enhancement in sensitivity, with confidence levels of 95% exceeding a Higgs boson mass threshold of 40 GeV. The study also considers a scenario in which a light scalar boson is produced in the decay of a top quark, with a mass difference between the Higgs and light scalar boson below 15 GeV.
