Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactic information, yet their use for syntax parsing has proved difficult. This study demonstrates that a successful self-supervised syntax parsing approach can emerge from a trained language model without the need for handcrafted word tag features or the labor-intensive creation of annotated parses, which previous methods rely on heavily. Instead, we found that a few syntax parsing tasks, around five, along with an effective way to translate those tags, allow for the creation of a universal parser that can accurately tag new tasks, given just a handful of examples. Furthermore, a new training strategy was developed to increase the number of available tasks, thereby facilitating the process. As a result, the creation of new tasks, previously a labor-intensive process, can now be done automatically, along with the accurate tagging of new tasks, even with minimal annotated data. This achievement surpasses other current methods, even when handcrafted features and more annotated data are used.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) technology. Despite advancements in ASR, the available solutions are limited by high costs, proprietary restrictions, and subpar performance on specific accents or languages. To address these challenges, we introduce Kaldi-De, a 4.7% word error rate deep neural network for the more complex German language, trained on open-source data and available for integration with other low-cost ASR models, such as the Kaldi-De model's performance is comparable to the industry-leading Kenlm-ASR model, a neural network-based system that has been optimized through data enhancement and architectural improvements.

The 30 Doradur HII region in the Large Magellanic Cloud is home to 52 Be-type stars, a significant number, and we have conducted a detailed analysis of their properties. Utilizing Gaia's EDR3 data, we were able to calculate the distances of 42 of these stars, with their distances matching the 30 Doradur HII region's distance within 1 kpc precision. We found that these stars' masses range from 10 to 20 M$_\odot$, with a median value of 14.5 M$_\odot$. The stars exhibit signs of mass loss, and our analysis revealed that 30 Doradur HII contains the highest number of Be-type stars known, along with distinct characteristics. Furthermore, we observed that nitrogen-rich stars tend to be located in densely populated areas.

To enhance the efficiency of spoken language systems, inverse text normalization needs to convert written numbers back into their textual form accurately and quickly. Traditional methods using templates have limitations in handling complex formats and low variations of written numbers. A more advanced approach utilizes deep neural networks to learn patterns from existing data, but still faces challenges with diverse formats and limited data. Our solution to this problem involves leveraging data augmentation to create additional training samples by combining written numbers with their correct text representations. By training our model on this augmented data, we have seen significant improvements in its performance, ultimately achieving a 37% decrease in error rate compared to existing models.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue 
of the Hermite operator when subject to Robin boundary conditions, showing 
that the optimal configuration is a half-space, and investigates the conditions 
under which equality occurs.

Deep neural networks, specifically those with a kernel architecture, are a prominent class of models. Kernels, being highly sensitive to their input, are heavily influenced by a few critical data points, known as support vectors, which heavily dictate their behavior. In this study, we propose a method to release these support vectors, allowing the kernel classifiers to be updated with new data without retraining, thus enabling truly continuous learning. Our method has been successfully tested on several real-world datasets, including text classification and image recognition tasks, and we provide a methodological comparison of our approach with other online learning techniques, showcasing its superiority in our experiments.

In recent years, a type of topological structure called non-Hermitian point-gap topology has gained significant attention, primarily due to its robust nature against disorder and fluctuations. However, the impact of correlations on such systems remains poorly understood. We investigate the effect of correlations on the point-gap topology in one-dimensional su(2) systems and two systems inspired by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings demonstrate that correlations can eliminate non-Hermitian point-gap topology by shifting the system from a topological to a trivial state, driven by interactions. The location where this transition occurs is determined by a method that combines the study of braided fermions and the use of the density matrix renormalization group. Our research highlights the critical role correlations play in shaping the topological properties of systems with non-Hermitian point-gap topology.

Our current research builds upon our earlier findings where we synthesized speech with social attributes such as gender and age. We've expanded this work to incorporate not only gender and age, but also an additional factor - accent. We've developed a novel approach using the XLS-R model, a pre-trained XLS-R model, to incorporate these social attributes in synthetic speech. This approach involves the use of a textual description of speaker characteristics to identify and incorporate a speaker's personal voice characteristics. We've explored using social attributes as a means of disambiguating speakers and have demonstrated that our system is successful at accurately identifying and matching speakers based on the content and associated speaker characteristics provided in the input text.

A radiative seesaw model incorporating light dark matter and featuring modular A4 and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries is proposed. The dark matter model with U(1) dark matter-coupling interactions is studied in the context of U(1)_(B-L) extension of the standard model. The co-annihilation of nucleons and the dark matter particle in the early universe is considered, which results in a larger effective annihilation rate and alleviates constraints on the dark matter parameter space. Furthermore, modular U(1)_(A) symmetry is shown to suppress lepton flavour violation, resulting in better agreement with the current experimental bounds on this phenomenon.

This study focuses on the quantum characteristics of nuclei with a non-uniform spatial framework. Building upon a previously established framework, we have made the Deformed Harmonic Oscillator conceptually deformed. Consequently, we have re-evaluated deformed oscillator concepts in this context. For nuclei with a non-uniform spatial framework, we examine their motion patterns in three dimensions. Initially, we examine how these patterns behave in a non-uniform 3D space, specifically in terms of Deformed HO and Collective HO. Subsequently, we investigate how the deformed HO shell structure evolves into a collective HO structure in nuclei with a non-uniform and deformed spatial framework. Furthermore, we explore the conditions under which nuclei with a non-uniform and deformed spatial framework exhibit collective motion. Our calculations utilize the Deformed HO model in a non-uniform 3D space to evaluate the B(E2) transition rates, which are found to be in good agreement with experimental observations.

Recently, Golay complementary matrices have experienced a resurgence due to their utility in sonar, radar, and wireless communication technologies. Yet, their available applications remain limited. This work extends polophase Golay complementary sequences to higher-dimensional structures, specifically polyphase Golay complementary arrays (GCA), which generalize Golay complementary matrices. Multiple GCAs constructions are presented utilizing various GCAs, particularly those based on complementary pairs. Notably, it is shown that CGC and PCRC, two specific GCAs, can be combined using Hadamard operations to form new GCAs. Furthermore, existing GCAs can be transformed into other GCAs via non-zero shifting. Two additional methods for generating GCAs are proposed: one involves Golay complementary matrices and the other relies on conjugate-paired Golay complementary matrices. Finally, computational examples are provided to validate the proposed constructions.

Incorporating dimensionality reduction techniques, such as PCA, ePCAO, and SSA, has proven beneficial in the field of hyperspectral imaging. Researchers have utilized these techniques in various contexts, such as hyperspectral images denoising. In the context of Change Detection (CD), our approach involves fusing these techniques in a deep Convolutional Autoencoder framework. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through the analysis of the well-known Los Angeles dataset. The results indicate that our method achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art CD methods, resulting in higher Kappa values and enhanced visual quality. Furthermore, it is worth noting that our method is unsupervised, which distinguishes it from other CD techniques.

Using computational simulations, researchers have found a connection between the residual entropy of a fluid and its viscosity, applicable to various conditions. Similar to the well-known relation between temperature and viscosity (Arrhenius law), residual entropy and viscosity also exhibit a consistent pattern. This correlation holds true for different conditions, including those with negative pressure, and across a range of molecular models, including argon, CO2, and methane. The experimentally observed viscosity values for CO2 and methane also align with the predicted relationship based on simulated residual entropy.

The most successful model, $\Lambda CDM$, has seen the introduction of various $\Lambda CDM$-based model periodicity studies. A theoretical framework is established to assess such analyses in the context of specific data and observation constraints. It is demonstrated that periodic assessments can be misleading in the absence of statistical tests, which may indicate bias or specific model choices. A new periodicity study in the $\Lambda CDM$ model using the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method is presented. Results align with the expected $\Lambda CDM$ model prior to parameter inference and show a consistent posterior period that is, however, not supported by the data. It is concluded that periodicity analysis in the $\Lambda CDM$ model requires a shift in approach to avoid misleading outcomes.

A new superdeterministic theory Invariant-set theory has been proposed in recent years by J. A. Vilarino. Some key features of this theory are its claim that all physical systems operate on a superdeterministic background known as the invariant set, along with its alignment with M theory. A comprehensive analysis of this theory is conducted within the hidden-variable framework through the use of the CHSH inequality. The study concludes with speculation about potential research directions for further investigation into this theory.

We examine Neural Networks (NNs) for keyword spotting on IoT devices, 
focusing on the constraints of these devices in running NNs and how it impacts their design.
Key considerations include reducing computational requirements, memory usage, and the impact of these constraints on design.
We examine a type of NN called quantized neural networks and how this type can accommodate IoT devices within their limitations, 
involving model parameters and computational complexity. We create a type of verifiable computation framework to demonstrate how NN inference under quantization, 
involving both training and inference, can be completed within the memory of an IoT device. We also explore how to utilize the cloud for NN inference when device memory is insufficient, 
involving a partial NN splitting strategy to divide the model between the device and cloud based on the available memory. Our approach aims to accommodate various NN quantization strategies and can be applied to multiple IoT devices. Our method's aim is to accommodate NNs to various IoT devices' memory, whether it's the available memory or the device's memory after a function call.

In the case of a gauge field with non-zero curvature, the issues of critical dimer and eight-vertex loop models are shown to be connected to the behavior of a Weyl fermion interacting with the gauge field. By employing the Pauli-Villars regularization technique, we find that the fermion's interaction with the gauge field results in an entropy correction corresponding to the lattice model's statistical mechanics partition function. Additionally, we find that the lattice model's action includes a topological term matching the fermion's action in two dimensions. In the scenario where gauge curvature is non-trivial, we find that curvature dependence arises in the fermion's action and can be explained as the cost of regulating the dimer model's partition function in the presence of a background gauge field.

Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse estimation in model prediction can be complex. The Group Lasso method, particularly effective for handling such data, has several limitations, including a data preprocessing step that can be computationally expensive for large datasets and the inability to guarantee a unique model due to group parameter symmetry. The Fixed-Effects Group Lasso and Relaxed-PEGLasso methods were developed to overcome these limitations, offering unique model estimation and group effects measurement capabilities. Our proposed algorithm combines these methods into the Fixed-PEGL, enabling unique model estimation and superior performance through significant improvement in accuracy metrics such as precision, recall, and the area under the ROC curve, along with efficient computation and the ability to handle large datasets.

To ensure the reliability of embedded systems, we suggest improving multiple existing approaches.  A single hypothesis addresses system verification errors by guaranteeing group scheduling.  Another solution uses a isolated memory area to guarantee the reliability of critical applications.  A more in-depth review reveals these strategies have a unresolved scheduling uncertainty.  A more reliable system utilising ARM hardware support has been developed, combining co-scheduling with virtual memory isolation technologies.  A more in-depth analysis of real-time capabilities under various critical situations has been conducted on this platform.  A more in-depth simulation of resource sharing issues has demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed solution, significantly reducing verification errors and ensuring group scheduling certainty.

When taking panoramic selfies with friends, the perspective distortion can result in exaggerated facial features due to varying heights. For example, taking a selfie from the waist often exaggerates height differences more than shooting from the eyes. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach to stitching high-resolution images into panoramic selfies at a minimal perspective angle. By shooting images from a wide angle and using a gravity-based algorithm to position key points, the approach avoids the complexities of image alignment. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of high-quality panoramic selfies featuring people with diverse body types.

When two coupled populations with uniform distribution of individual tunability parameters are considered, with one population having a fixed number of members, the other's average participation can vary freely, a "chimera state" can occur, under specific conditions involving tunability and synchronization. However, if the participating size of the second population is close to its total number of members, no clear-synchronized, in-phase relationship exists. Through further analysis using mathematical tools such as energy functions and normal-form maps, the phase portrait displays distinct patterns that differ from the typical coexistence of in-phase and out-of-phase states. We define and describe the two distinct types of stable, out-of-phase relationship that can occur.

In practical situations, controllers are exposed to unexpected disturbances, prompting the need for more robust solutions. While controllers can be designed to be disturbance-repelling, the standard approach lacks the ability to predict which controller will be more resilient. Based on control-affine systems, we propose a probabilistic model for control systems that accounts for disturbance impacts. This model can learn from data collected while the controller interacts with the system, and is capable of quantifying robustness by estimating the effect of disturbances on performance. Using this model, we can identify the most robust controller without requiring extensive simulation or physical testing. Our approach is validated on control tasks of generating a double pendulum's eigenfunctions and managing the X-ray free-electron laser at MAXLAB.

We present a multi-layer quiver in this paper, using which we can build a higher dimension (n+1) algebras of infinite complexity from a given n-dimensional one. This process enables the transformation of a higher dimension algebras of finite complexity into one of higher dimension and higher complexity. Our study focuses on the construction of quivers for n-dimensional quiver algebras and results in a new class of infinite dimensional algebras that have higher dimension algebras of finite complexity and n + 1 hereditary components. These algebras are a generalisation of the slice algebras first introduced by Telschow.

We investigate reflected entropy, a lower bound on entanglement entropy that can detect phase transitions, in random tensor networks. By utilizing this tool, we can distinguish between two distinct quantum phases within this framework: a volume law phase and an area law phase. Moreover, we calculate a scaling factor, $\gamma$, that quantifies the difference in reflected entropy between these phases. The value of $\gamma$ corresponds to the ratio of the geometric lengths between specific boundaries in the network. Furthermore, we analyze how reflected entropy behaves when certain qubits are measured and find its difference between the two phases to be directly proportional to the number of such qubits. These findings demonstrate the unique sensitivity of reflected entropy to the underlying structure of random tensor networks.

Living organisms' success relies on passing genetic information to ensure the continuity of life patterns over time. In contrast, traditional theoretical frameworks have not provided a clear explanation for how information is preserved in living systems. We introduce a new approach that identifies heritable structures within stochastic systems by identifying solutions that maintain their identity over time. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its discovery of enduring patterns within non-equilibrium systems, such as the 2D Ising model, and in a wide variety of gene regulatory networks, particularly those based on double negative feedback loops. Notably, our approach reveals that many such networks display remarkable stability over extended periods.

We investigate the dynamics of a basic 3D version of the H\'{e}non map by varying its control parameters, and observe its movement from simple, predictable behavior to complex, complex patterns including chaotic movement. Using basic techniques for basic map analysis in combination with cutting, crushing, and stretching methods, we map out the structures of these complex patterns in the parameter space. Our results are compared with the well-studied H\'{e}non-Sparrow map, which is also modified in the same way.

We analyze the statistical behavior of two specific types of hook lengths in lambda-partitioned sets, focusing on the cases where the hook lengths are multiples of two or three. Our findings are supported by specific equations for both scenarios.

Quantum fluctuations in tunneling particles can result in a delay in tunneling, which occurs due to the Larmor clock mechanism and has a distinct, spin-fluctuation-based tunneling time, differing from other types of tunneling times. We aim to explore the role spin fluctuations play in tunneling time, T-scheme approach in a two-state tunneling model with dephasing. Within this framework, our research indicates that spin fluctuations can be in balance with energy for symmetric barriers, which leads to the possibility of the total tunneling time being roughly equal to the sum of energy-based and spin-based contributions. We aim to examine the potential for the total tunneling time being equal to the sum of energy-based and spin-based contributions, which may occur in specific tunneling conditions, including those involving recollision and under certain asymmetric barriers with varying spin-based tunneling times.

This research investigates the leading twist distribution amplitudes of non-relativistic P-wave mesons. By utilizing model-independent sum rules, it determines the leading twist distribution amplitude of a non-relativistic P-wave meson. Furthermore, it examines key properties, such as asymptotic amplitudes, asymmetry parameters, and sum rule coefficients. Lastly, it employs sum rules to calculate the twist-3 distribution amplitude, along with its long-term behavior coefficient $E_2(\beta)$.

Researchers have proposed an approach to implement nonlinear quantum gates using Bose-Einstein condensates. This method involves excitation of BEC through acoustic waves and achieving specific particle numbers in different sound modes, which enables the realization of a nonlinear phase shift between the modes. However, a nonzero phase shift can only be achieved when a certain condition is met, based on Bessel function properties. Additionally, a theoretical model suggests that a specific trap configuration can lead to the cancellation of Bessel function zeros, further enhancing the nonlinear phase shift between modes.

The extended BMS algebra incorporating rotations and translations will be introduced, leading to the interpretation of a specific class of diffeomorphisms at future null infinity as zero-mode currents of a 2D conformal field theory, a concept further explored using a holographic model. The anti-de Scentred Green function (AdS) decoupling limit of the Wess-Zumino-Witten model, with specific central charges, will be decoupled and demonstrated to yield a 2d conformal field theory based on the extended BMS algebra. Soft photon and graviton scattering amplitudes will be derived from conserved charges through the exchange of virtual stress tensor, revealing their equivalence to double soft limits, and provide a different perspective on the process. These findings can be applied to flat space AdS and demonstrate how soft photons and gravitons can be connected to secondary states, with the amplitudes being derived using a holographic model. These findings can be applied to the flat space.

Learning with an ever-growing number of categories poses significant challenges, particularly when it comes to handling large-scale data streams. The task of Online Ensemble Continual Learning is further complicated when it comes to situations where categories increase continuously, without any opportunity for model retraining from scratch. To tackle this problem, researchers have proposed an novel neural architecture called NEfA that excels in handling Online CE tasks by leveraging previously learned knowledge from multiple towers, each trained on different categories. By utilizing shared memory, NeFa enables the adaptation of towers to new tasks while retaining knowledge from old tasks. NeFa's ability to adapt towers on the fly and store them in the memory, without the need for excessive computational resources, sets it apart from other approaches. To demonstrate its effectiveness, NeFa has been successfully applied to a range of benchmark datasets, including MNIST, EMNIST, CIFAR10, and ImageNet, and has also been applied to the popular Online Learning Benchmarks, beating the state-of-the-art results by notable margins.

In our research, we establish a novel approach for constructing Einstein metrics by utilizing Generalized Complex and Complex Symmetric metrics as an extension of the traditional Complex Hermitian metrics. This approach enables us to develop a unified framework for Extended Ricci Flat four-metrics, combining previously proposed Ricci Flat metrics on four-dimensional spaces. This method ultimately proves effective and efficient in generating new Einstein metrics, while also forming the foundation for future research aimed at finding complete solutions to the Einstein equation through the application of the generalized complex approach.

In the wake of several recently constructed permutation polynomials over finite fields with square orders, our focus shifts to analyzing permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders through a detailed examination of their coefficients. Utilizing the multivariate method and resultant elimination, we establish complete permutation polynomials over finite fields with cube orders and calculate their leading terms, subsequently determining the count of such permutation polynomials.

Deep learning techniques, specifically Deep Belief Networks, have shown significant potential in automatic classification tasks, including image classification. This paper describes a deep learning model used for classifying intestinal parasites from microscopy images, replacing traditional, time-consuming methods with automated image analysis. The model achieves a 94% accuracy on a testing dataset and demonstrates promising results for parasite classification, with further improvements possible by replacing the top layer and utilizing image preprocessing techniques.

This work introduces a novel approximation technique for a broad category of zero-sum-free stochastic differential investment and reinsurance models. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs value functions, a tensor train representation is utilized. This technique offers computational efficiency and approximates the tensor data in the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs system's coefficients. By doing so, it effectively addresses the complexity of tensor data. An algorithm is devised to solve the resulting tensor data-approximated equation. Furthermore, the method's effectiveness and accuracy are demonstrated through examples.

This research presents a novel Proportional-Integral-Derivative-Acceleration (PIDA) approach for optimizing Multi-Rotor Robot trajectories in real-time dual algorithm setup. The proposed method utilizes a derivative acceleration term for accelerating dual simplex algorithm convergence. For real-time execution, a modified dual simplex algorithm is introduced with a stable algorithm. Additionally, a new derivative observer based on stochastic dual dynamic programming algorithm for real-time control. The algorithm's stability is proven through Lyapunov theory. The algorithm's effectiveness is also demonstrated through a genetic filter for real-time state estimation. The algorithm's performance is evaluated through simulated experiments and live drone flights, showcasing the ability to achieve smooth and stable flight paths.

A comprehensive review of recent pion-nucleon interaction research is presented, with a focus on low-energy regions. The discussion encompasses both experimental data and theoretical frameworks, drawing connections to chiral effective field theory, symmetry breaking, and QCD. The assessment highlights key achievements, fundamental issues, and computational methods employed for low-energy scattering, as well as constraints on the pion-nucleon sigma term.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is designed to gather more data than its predecessor by incorporating 20 additional pixel detectors. These new detectors, known as Pilot Slabs, were integrated into the CMS Pixel system in 2008 and have been processing data from the CMS Phase-1 upgrade. A reconstruction algorithm was developed for these pilot slabs, which is adapted from the main CMS detector but tailored to fit the new hardware. This paper outlines the details of the algorithm and presents its evaluation using data from proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV with an unprecedented amount of data, 10 petabytes. It also describes the results of running this software on pilot slabs embedded within the CMS detector.

We have developed a machine learning model to classify active galactic nucleus host galaxies into three types: elliptical, disk, and irregular. The model is based on 14 years of data from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and achieves accurate results for galaxies with observations spanning 14 years. The model's performance is evaluated using the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey data, and it is compared to traditional color-based methods. The classification system is further refined by incorporating morphological data from the Galaxy Zoo project. The study reveals that the point-source subtraction process in the Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging data successfully removes active galactic nucleus data, resulting in reliable galaxy morphology measurements. The findings indicate that the measured morphologies of galaxies in our sample are in good agreement with those from the Galaxy Zoo project.

High-energy and high-momentum interactions within nuclear matter are largely governed by short-range correlations, specifically denoted as nucleon-nucleon correlations, characterized by distances under 1 femtometer and relative momenta exceeding 400 MeV/c. The research presents various nuclear nuclear short-range correlations (nSC) distributions, including those of the $^{12}$C nucleus, which are represented through different models, with the Mott model, mott-type (MT) and the light-front (LF) wave function providing a more detailed and accurate picture. The results of this study show that nSC distribution is highly sensitive to the wave function used, with the LF wave function revealing a broader distribution in terms of both transverse and longitudinal momentum, as well as a distinct shape in the $q$-$2k$ distribution, which peaks at lower values of $q$ compared to the Mott and mott-type distributions, thereby allowing for more precise identification of nSC. The findings also suggest that the nSC distribution observed in the E12a experiment and recently measured data from the EMC experiment can be best explained by the light-front distribution. The research further indicates that the mott-type and Mott distributions may not be able to reproduce the parabolic dependence of normalized yields observed in various experiments and may not be able to explain a significant portion of the data from the Mott cross-section measurements and the structure functions of the EMC experiment, while the LF wave function, specifically

Deep neural networks excel in solving real-world problems efficiently due to their remarkable flexibility and adaptability, but they are hindered by the vast number of parameters and the lengthy training process when dealing with large datasets. A significant factor contributing to their success lies in their ability to capture underlying patterns within data through learnable representations. Introducing symmetries into neural architectures can help mitigate the aforementioned challenges by significantly reducing the number of independent parameters. Complex numbers, possessing inherent phase symmetry, have proven to be particularly useful in representing complex data such as time-series, spectral signals, and speech signals. However, most complex-valued neural networks focus on imaginary symmetry and neglect the influence of phase symmetry in the output domain, where real and imaginary components are mixed and dependent on the phase angle. We propose the novel concept of co-domain symmetry, where a novel complex-sigmoid activation function is incorporated into neural networks to preserve co-domain structure, and demonstrate its superiority to traditional complex-valued activation functions through experiments. The application of co-domain symmetry leads to significant reductions in independent parameters and the creation of more compact and efficient architectures, and our results show that the resulting models are on par with state-of-the-art models.

The non-linear QCD evolution equations ultimately lead to the formation of a distinct region in phase space where saturation effects can be observed experimentally.  Saturated target parameters can be estimated in terms of two key variables: one being the nuclear modification factor $R_{AA}$ and the other being $p_T$ in heavy ion collisions, or $x_B$ and $z$ for deep inelastic electron-proton and electron-nucleus collisions, respectively.  Given measurable constraints on $p_T$ in heavy ion collisions or $z$ for deep inelastic collisions, experiments can determine whether saturation effects are taking place by checking for a specific dependence of $x_B$ on the saturation parameter $x_{\text{Sat}}$.  We explore and compare the saturation mechanisms in deep inelastic and heavy ion collisions.

A thorough study of the Galactic halo's stellar population was conducted across a broad abundance range. By analyzing 18 different abundance ratios, 109 stars were examined within a specific metallicity and baryon density interval using a newly developed code. To assess agreement with $\Lambda$CDM, a statistical test was applied to the abundance data, along with an analysis of the Galactic halo's chemical development. Key factors influencing abundance variability were identified, including a significant role for oxygen abundance and a significant contribution from $^{12}$C/$^{18}$O. The results support chemical evolution models that align with chemical homogeneity, particularly in elements like Sr, Y, Zr, and Ba, and indicate that r-process enrichment occurred early in the Galaxy. However, notable scatter remains in the Fe/H and [Fe/α] ratios, and a significant spread was observed in the Mg/α and Si/α abundance ratios.

A novel machine learning approach has been developed to measure the stability of predictive models against changes in input data, known as sensitivity. Using the SMS Spam Collection dataset as a test case, this method effectively measures the stability of model predictions, even in scenarios where data exhibits strong dependencies. A key finding is that our sensitivity technique can identify and address weak spots in model performance. When evaluating financial literacy prediction models using the A4C dataset, our method revealed significant variability in performance depending on specific data subsets. Consequently, our research proposes targeted interventions to mitigate sources of inconsistency and enhance model reliability.

This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing SQUID to integrate seamlessly into PyTorch ML workflows. Various hybrid models are provided out-of-the-box in SQUID to facilitate comparison and experimentation. Several classification tasks are accomplished using SQUID to demonstrate its capabilities.

Researchers, Chen and Garay, have examined pointwise slant submanifolds in almost Hermitian manifolds. This study delves into pointwise semi-slant warped product submanifolds of almost contact manifolds. We establish a key result showing that for a pointwise semi-slant warped product manifold meeting certain conditions, its gradiente is constrained within a specific interval.

The PALEOCCENE concept has the potential to develop sensitive and efficient low-energy detectors that can operate at room temperature and are minimally maintained. Such detectors could range in size from single-molecule precision to large-scale industrial production, making them versatile tools for various applications, including low-energy physics and nuclear recoil detection, which could potentially test theories such as dark matter. Color centers could replace traditional detectors, such as those made of liquid argon, and instead, offer a more efficient and sensitive detection system. To explore this concept further, we propose the PALEOCCENE approach as a novel path toward advanced low-energy particle detection.

We examine a suspension of active colloids that interact with an externally imposed flow produced by nearby objects, creating an uneven distribution of activity levels. The effect of this external force on the suspension is studied through variations in its properties and structure, including particle positioning, density, and temperature, as well as the assembly of particles into ordered patterns. To achieve this arrangement, we propose a method for applying torque to individual particles or groups of particles to modify their behavior in response to the uneven activity levels. The results show that a net alignment of particles occurs, facilitated by torque application, which has significant implications for controlling heat transfer and viscosity within the suspension, as well as its potential use in directed transport and energy conversion applications.

We investigate numerically the sum rules for optical conductivity within the context of a fractional quantum Hall insulator, utilizing both a particle-hole excitation model and a magnetoroton model in order to gain a deeper understanding of its spectral characteristics. By applying a recently developed approach, we identify a non-perturbative contribution to the spectrum that arises from incompressible background fluctuations, encompassing both deep and shallow states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optical conductivity spectrum is composed of a inelastic peak and a relatively weak background, with both features accurately accounted for by the magnetoroton model. Notably, at intermediate frequencies where deep states are inaccessible, a significant discrepancy arises between the predictions of the magnetoroton model and exact results, thereby revealing the essential role of deep states in shaping the system's spectral sum rules.

Epidemics on complex network structures offer a captivating intersection of theoretical physics and data science applications, encompassing diverse fields from communications to finance. By applying concepts of data clustering, it's possible to simplify the simulation and analysis of such epidemics through a proposed geometric approach. This involves transforming a graph into a space of a specific simplex, which facilitates the use of a clustering algorithm to divide the original network into distinct subgroups. Subsequently, an algorithm is introduced to restore the initial network from these subgroups. The authors demonstrate the efficacy of this method with a case study on the reconstruction of a 1,000 node network from its epidemic dynamics, which they verify using a physics-based model.

A straightforward and versatile approach is presented to minimize artifacts in maps created using maximum likelihood methods with weighted source catalogs. These artifacts, often seen as intersecting lines of negative amplitude, arise when scanning around the sources of the cosmic microwave background radiation. This method can incorporate both on- and off-source observations without altering the source weights. When implemented, the algorithm effectively eliminates artifacts in simulated maps and has been utilized in preliminary cosmological parameter analysis. Our approach can be adapted to handle catalogs that are not yet available.

Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be challenging due to the complexity of understanding the meaning of individual words and phrases. This issue becomes even more complicated when dealing with visual states that contain multiple objects of the same type. Prior research has explored using language in goal-conditioned reinforcement learning models, often incorporating language to describe objectives, but typically focusing on understanding word meanings rather than how those words apply to actual visual states. Our research focuses on a more fundamental problem - accurately identifying which object a teacher intends to refer to - and proposes two approaches to improve this - using language descriptions of visual features and representing the subjective characteristics of a teacher. Through thorough testing in both simple and complex environments, we demonstrate that teachers can utilize this knowledge to resolve ambiguities and enhance their teaching efficiency.

Quantum information theory's fundamental concept of channel discarding is key to understanding quantum coherence and coherence-related phenomena. However, experimentally discarding a black box quantum channel poses a challenge, necessitating new strategies for relevant discards. We introduce a novel strategy for implementing shadow process tomography, utilizing measurement and classical post-processing of process matrices. This new strategy, based on maximum entropy, maintains compatibility with existing tomographic methods for process matrices. Our experimentally validated protocol illustrates its potential in characterizing quantum channels, particularly Ivanovic's not-universal NOT channel, through successful measurement of the process matrix of a real-world noisy channel implementing a soliton free-induction decay.

We aim to derive precise bounds for the Cheeger constant using a range of geometric attributes such as area, perimeter, inradius, circumradius, minimum width and diameter. Our approach involves establishing tight inequalities among these measures specifically for planar convex bodies, along with formulating sharp bounds across various dimensions. Furthermore, we successfully prove long-standing conjectures regarding the Cheeger constant of planar convex sets proposed by several experts including J. Rauch, S. Talbot, A. Figalli, G. Ponce and A. G. Andreasi Bologni.

This study investigates trajectory planning for aerial drones in situations requiring time-sensitive execution within a specified timeframe.
The optimization problem is formulated as minimizing energy consumption while adhering to the maximum drone speed constraint.
The issue of trajectory optimization is initially complex and can't be easily resolved when including additional physical constraints, like the drones acceleration constraint.
The problem is thus decomposed into two manageable sub-problems: a time scheduling problem and a trajectory estimation problem.
The time scheduling problem is complex and non-linear; however, it can be converted into minimizing the inverse of a convex function by eliminating speed constraints.
To address this complexity, the study employs a dual decomposition method to produce an optimal solution, while a modified penalty method is used to derive an approximate solution when this technique isn't applicable.
To resolve the second subproblem and obtain the trajectory given the scheduled time points, the problem is divided into smaller sub-optimal trajectory problems, and these are solved iteratively.
The effectiveness of the proposed approach is verified through simulation, revealing significant speed improvements over traditional dynamic programming, particularly for larger numbers of drones and tasks.

The low-energy electronic structure of a complex bilayer graphene system, consisting of two parabolic bands, is analyzed using the renormalization group approach. Focusing on the Coulomb interaction within this system, we identify the emergence of four distinct types of Fermi-liquid vertex operators at the linearized renormalization group fixed point. These operators are then tracked through the renormalization group flow, and we discover that an unstable parabolic point can lead to instability and potential phase transitions within the bilayer graphene ground state. Our results demonstrate that upon introducing subleading Coulomb interaction channels, the instability is diminished. Consequently, we propose that unstable bilayer graphene can potentially exhibit non-Fermi-liquid and deconfined quantum critical behavior. Furthermore, we draw parallels with the tight-binding model of a free massless Dirac fermion in $(3+1)$-dimensional spacetime, suggesting areas for further research.

The conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 on h-BN/Ni(111) undergos significant changes due to variations in temperature, specifically switching between the 4h and 6h structures within the temperature range of 150-300 K. Experimental data obtained through scanning tunneling microscopy, combined with density functional theory calculations, reveal that at 150 K, molecules predominantly exist in the 4h structure, whereas above 200 K, a dynamic equilibrium is established between the 4h and 6h configurations. Moreover, a distinct arrangement of dimers on the surface, linked by short distances, is evident at temperatures above 200 K. Additionally, a notable difference in tunneling current intensity between the inner and outer spheres of the molecules is also observed, with the inner sphere's tunneling current significantly higher. Lastly, a clear correlation between the molecular arrangement and the underlying hexagonal holes of h-BN is also evident, with a notable hole filling phenomenon observed along the dimer connection.

The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various low-powered IoT devices such as sensors and actuators, communicating over a network to share data. Due to these devices' network connectivity, they present vulnerable targets for data theft and other cyber threats. As a result, implementing data protection measures like encryption is crucial for securing IoT devices against such threats. However, conventional encryption methods pose a substantial processing challenge for resource-constrained IoT devices. In an effort to overcome this limitation, this paper evaluates various lightweight encryption algorithms, which include AES-ECB, AES-CBC, ChaCha20-Poly1305, Simeck64, SPN, and PRESENT, to determine their suitability for protecting data on low-powered IoT devices.

The Ramsey sequence serves as a prime illustration of quantum phase measurement, and its efficiency in measurements has prompted its application to a myriad of problems. Nevertheless, its suitability for experiments involving small sample sizes is limited to date, largely due to its primary focus on precision rather than optimal resource allocation. Our research introduces a novel strategy for planning Ramsey sequence experiments by adapting principles from Bayesian statistics. We employ a Bayesian framework to quantify the probabilistic nature of phase measurements, and we derive a Bayesian phase estimator that allows us to quantify estimation uncertainty. By maximizing the expected log-likelihood of the phase estimate, we establish a decision-making criterion that guides the experimental process. We demonstrate the utility of our approach through simulations, showing that it can reduce variance in estimation accuracy, and we extend its feasibility for real-world experiments.

Network centrality metrics assess node importance by analyzing relationships between direct and indirect connections. The Gromov centrality metric evaluates centrality based on the disparity between direct and indirect paths for a given node, combining both local and global network characteristics. The Gromov centrality was applied to four distinct networks, comparing it to existing metrics and demonstrating its capability to capture both tight-knit and loosely connected node characteristics and community role characteristics.

To address the long-standing "missing link" issue in quark physics, specifically regarding the symmetric distribution of quarks within hadrons, and in comparison with the standard model of electroweak interactions, an author proposes a symmetric distribution of photons in an azimuthally symmetric electromagnetic field. This concept is used to derive new field equations incorporating spinors, and applied to azimuthally symmetric sources to generate corresponding spinor solutions. A specific scenario with source pressure is considered, and efforts are made to solve the resulting system of non-linear differential equations numerically.

Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups of bundles, characterized by a common set of invariant polynomials. This classification is facilitated by new findings on certain generalized Sylvester equations, whose solutions define numerically stable algorithms for determining these invariants. We introduce specific criteria that enable the creation of bundles consisting of matrix pencils with identical Kronecker canonical forms, allowing for the comparison of these structures through invariants. The concept of resolutive matrix pencils is also defined.

The $C^*$-algebra formalism of topological T-duality developed by Mathai and Rosenberg is applied to a broad class of topological spaces encompassing torus bundles, nilmanifolds, and other examples from string theory. By constructing T-duals from commutative $C^*$-algebras defined on these spaces, it is shown that T-duality arises from a dual group action involving a Lie group. This dual $C^*$-algebra is explicitly calculated and provides significant insights into understanding T-duals of torus bundle foliations within the context of noncommutative geometry.

Our investigation involves plotting a minor-free metric space with a limited number of vertices, measuring the distortion in terms of its g-minor-free upper bound and its treewidth, which involves a negative exponent. This problem is related to previous work on efficiently embedding certain graphs into others with limited distortion. Specifically, we focus on the case of the outerplanar graphs, which have a known distortion bound when embedded into a cycle graph with a number of vertices proportional to the graph's own. For the more general class of minor-free graphs, we develop an algorithm that embeds such graphs into a cycle with a number of vertices proportional to the graph's own, achieving a bound on the distortion in terms of the graph's own variables and its treewidth. This result has an interesting consequence when applied to the minor-free graphs themselves, involving variables related to the graph's own minor upper bound and its treewidth. This result is further improved for the specific case of the graphs formed by removing the edges of a projective planar graph, which have a known distortion bound when embedded into a cycle with a number of vertices proportional to the square root of the graph's own. This result has a known distortion bound when applied to the general case and is based on the notion of a graph's own variables and its distortion.

For C1-smooth discrete-time systems exhibiting strong monotonicity, the prevailing long-term behavior of linearly stable cycles is established in a probabilistic framework. This research then extends to periodic parabolic equations and reveals new findings regarding the ubiquity of periodic solution convergence. Notably, in Neumann-bound equations defined on convex domains, the set of initial conditions corresponding to periodic solutions is shown to be prevalent, while in radially symmetric domains, the set of radially symmetric initial conditions leads to periodic or cyclic parabolic convergence profiles.

The potential of quantum computers to accurately and efficiently solve complex equations is appealing, but current hardware is prone to errors. The development of "variational" algorithms, which are more resilient to errors, has been key in applying quantum technology in practical scenarios. A new variation of this technique has been proposed in the form of the QEAVQE algorithm, which combines the benefits of the traditional AVQE method with the capabilities of the quantum eigensolver. By focusing solely on the most critical parts of a molecule's electron structure, the QEAVQE algorithm achieves significant reductions in circuit complexity and resource requirements, enabling it to outperform the traditional AVQE method in terms of required circuits, resources, and number of measurements. This has been confirmed through theoretical and numerical studies of several examples, showing that even for challenging complex molecules, the new algorithm's superior performance is evident.

A key characteristic of deep generative models is the interaction of their representation and transformation components. Deep SINDs, specifically, evaluate a few key characteristics of a dataset by training a compact and efficient representation that effectively reduces complexity. By leveraging these model parameters, we can develop an effective classifier and estimator. However, relying solely on these parameters may be insufficient for tasks such as visualization and outlier detection, which typically require a functional encoder-decoder model. Previous studies have attempted to develop deep encoders-decoders, but often with limited success. By focusing on directly mapping high-level model parameters to a low-dimensional space, we can develop an effective deep encoder-decoder. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method on several tasks and compare our findings with traditional models.

The discovery of a common-spectrum process in recent NANOGrav findings could signify either evidence for a stochastic gravitational-wave background (GWBG) originating from the merger of binary pulsars or a "stiff" GWBG produced by quantum fluctuations during inflation, amplified due to a steep slope ($\alpha > 0.02$) between 10$^{-12}$ Hz and 10$^{-10}$ Hz. To determine the plausibility of this hypothesis, we examine the constraints set by LIGO-Virgo's non-observation of primordial black holes (PBHs) forming via cosmological density perturbations, and we derive an upper bound on the inflationary tilt ($|n_s - 1| < 0.02$) derived from the absence of GWBG detection by LIGO-Virgo, in addition to existing constraints on the tensor-to-curvature ratio ($r < 0.004$) derived from the Planck satellite. This discovery highlights the potential for GW detection to provide insights into the inflationary potential, in particular for "stiff" variants, and narrow down PBH formation via cosmological density perturbations.

Our study of molecular emissions in comet C/2015 ER61 PanSTARRS, observed using the ALMA Atacama Compact Array, revealed that CO, CN, and CO+ ions are predominantly emitted from the nucleus, as indicated by their observed flux profiles. Conversely, CH+, CO, and C2 ions appear to be emitted from a distributed area around the comet, as suggested by the best model fits. Analysis of the observed flux profiles and spectral line shapes, however, revealed that CO, CH+, and C2 ions are likely emitted from a distributed area, and not from the nucleus, with the source extending up to 150-200 km. Assuming a uniform gas release, our findings indicate that approximately 70% of these ions are emitted from this distributed area. Moreover, our observations of CO, CH+, and C2 ions, along with their corresponding flux profiles, reveal that CH+, CO, and C2 ions are produced through the sublimation of volatiles, rather than through their photodissociation, with the reaction rates of CH+, CO, and C2 ions being significantly lower than their expected values. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the mass loss rate of these comets is significantly lower than their expected values, with the mass loss rate of C/2015 ER61 PanSTARRS being estimated to be approximately 0.000000000000

We propose an unsupervised speech synthesis approach that builds on recent research using speaker vectors and phoneme embeddings, without the need for aligned transcripts. By leveraging phonemes from pre-trained models and a modified GAN-based voice approach, we demonstrate effective speech synthesis. Furthermore, we explore a method for automatically extracting speaker embeddings from unlabelled audio data through a two-step process. As demonstrated through subjective evaluations, our unsupervised system produces high-quality speech that is comparable to supervised systems based on the Mosaic voice algorithm.

This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy concept of Li and Wang (2014) to derive a novel complex-based quintessence model of dark energy and investigate its impact on the universe. We have simulated the dark energy field with varying phases, observing a direct correlation between these phases and the amplitude of complex scalar field ripples in the cosmos. These ripples, resulting from the stress-energy tensor's real component, influence cosmic structure formation. As a consequence, comparisons with cosmic microwave background radiation, baryon acoustic oscillations, and type Ia supernovae data reveal a less constrained equation of state parameter than in quintessence models utilizing conventional holographic dark energy. Notably, through the use of 1000 Monte Carlo simulations with 100 combined data sets, researchers found that the s parameter lies between -2.11 and 0.24 at 2-sigma confidence, significantly differing from quintessence models employing Tsallis holographic dark energy developed by Li and Wang (2014) with real exponents.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed to solve these problems efficiently. A comparison demonstrates the effectiveness of this method over the traditional branch-and-bound approach, with further illustration offered through a real-world mechanical engineering example.

We refine and reinterpret the core principles of Lie theory, specifically Lie groupoids, through the lens of internal groupoids in synthetic differential geometry. Key concepts are re-expressed, including path sources and integrated $A$-paths. The primary findings demonstrate that a classical Hausdorff Lie groupoid's internal connectivity implies it is internally connected and complete in an integral sense. This demonstrates a fundamental property--its 1-bifunctoriality--enables these internal properties to extend to composed Lie compositions.

The amount of secure, trustworthy, and proprietary biomedical data is growing rapidly, giving rise to a variety of challenges when trying to distribute it efficiently. Although technologies like blockchain and secure cloud computing have been developed to solve these issues, they have been difficult to implement in practice due to the need for substantial changes to existing workflows and policies. In this paper, we outline a strategy to create a gateway service that streamlines the sharing of proprietary biomedical data while maintaining its security and integrity. This innovative approach allows for seamless integration with various security technologies, as well as the management of blockchain-based trust relationships, all within a single, easy-to-use interface. By using a blockchain gateway, research collaborators can securely and effortlessly share proprietary data without having to go through complex implementation or policy changes, thus enhancing overall data sharing and collaboration.

Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews, and often employs Aspect Sentiment Orientation (ASO) tasks to achieve this. To improve accuracy in ASO tasks, many studies utilize extensive sentiment lexicons and predefined sentiment labels. However, pre-assigning these sentiments can inadvertently introduce a degree of ambiguity, and utilizing sentiment labels may not always be feasible in practice. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called contrastive pre-training for effective aspect representation learning without relying on predefined sentiment labels. Our method, referred to as ASO-Contrast, leverages a diverse range of positive, negative, and neutral aspects to simulate sentiment labels, thereby avoiding the need for extensive sentiment lexicons. Experimental evaluations conducted on various datasets confirm the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods.

We establish a method to calculate how sample fractions of cases and controls, direct influence, and media type identification contribute to research outcomes in large datasets, focusing on binary outcomes, population interventions, and binary intermediary factors in comprehensive datasets, filling a gap in statistical tools for studying media effects when cases and controls are sampled. As a result, our investigation yields precise formulas for estimating media effects from large datasets, along with estimation methods that can handle any sample from large datasets, data fractions, and binary intermediary factors that may have missing data. We illustrate the method's effectiveness in large datasets through numerical analysis.

This study proposes a reliable secure communication system that utilizes reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to manage uplink transmissions from multiple unstable sources to a single receiving station. Focusing on mixed-phased RIS elements and common source instability, we formulate an optimization issue to ensure the minimum required signal strength while keeping the total risk level below a specified threshold. Owing to the difficulty of solving this issue directly, we rephrase it into an equivalent problem that can be efficiently resolved through the use of an approximate approach. We further develop an iterative algorithm to tackle the resulting problem. Simulations confirm the system's effectiveness in mitigating common channel instability. The obtained results demonstrate that our proposed solution yields improved outcomes in terms of reliability. Notably, our findings reveal that risk minimization can be effectively addressed without the need for complicated non-linear algorithms.

We introduce a contrastive value policy that enables agents to improve their own knowledge by using a form of retrospective learning through summarization. By employing a contrastive value function, agents can contrast positive and negative forms of hindsight value and identify the most effective forms of useful learning activities. As a result, our approach empowers a RL agent to enhance its own knowledge by effectively engaging in self-improvement tasks. To support the feasibility of hindsight learning, we establish a theoretical framework for summarization and demonstrate its relevance to understanding based on information theory. Additionally, we provide findings suggesting that hypothesis testing and the use of inductive reasoning are critical value-based principles for enabling effective contrastive learning.

We analyzed the solar wind's energy flux at the inner heliosphere, specifically at orbital distances of around 15-30 million kilometers from the Sun, using data from 14 close encounters of the Parker Solar Probe between 2018 and 2020. The probe carried instruments capable of detecting high-frequency electric field fluctuations up to 100 kHz, providing a detailed view of the solar wind's energy spectrum, including both low-frequency magnetohydrodynamic waves and high-frequency field fluctuations. The observed large-field fluctuations were consistent with previous studies, but the first detections of high-frequency field fluctuations at such close distances to the Sun allowed us to calculate the total solar wind energy flux, combining the effects of both field fluctuation types. The results suggest that these field fluctuations decayed with a power of around 5.7-6.1 frequency units, and that their direction is consistent with theoretical expectations. The field fluctuations detected by the probe were found to contribute only a small fraction, less than 0.1 percent, to the total energy budget, while their magnitude was consistent with a radial decay of 1 over $r^{\frac{2}{3}}$. The obtained results provide new insights into the nature of these field fluctuations and their role in understanding the Sun's energy output.

In a noncommutative setting, where locally compact Hausdorff groups act on C*-algebras, we introduce the concept of a numerable principal bundle with quantum characteristics. This generalization involves replacing the locally compact Hausdorff space with the C*-algebra and the group with its associated groupoid. We also prove a noncommutative version of the well-known theorem stating that a numerable principal bundle on such a space is locally a product space.

We show that in models of ZFC, the ultrafilter number can be strictly greater than both the continuum and the almost disjointness number. This achieves a relationship between the almost disjointness number, the ultrafilter number, and the continuum, achieving a equality reminiscent of Cichon's sequence. Our method is based on a specific forcing iteration, starting with a club-preserving forcing. This starting point allows us to control the continuum and the almost disjointness number while making the ultrafilter number significantly higher, all in just $\omega_3$-many steps.

The line defect phenomenon in optical media, where increased transmission occurs at specific wavelengths, has been extensively studied. Researchers have found that having defects with varying refractive indices, all within the photonic bandgap's range, creates transparent windows at specific points, corresponding to the eigenmodes of the entire structure. These points exhibit enhanced group velocities due to the steep dispersion profile surrounding the bandgap. We investigate the possibility of achieving both transparency and enhanced group velocities in quantum-deformed optomechanical systems through numerical simulations of a specific system configuration.

In a two-rotor model where the two rotors behave as fermions, we examine negative-scission-negative (NSN) nature-1 scissors modes, which involve the negative R-parity. We consider two scenarios: the first where the rotors' angular momenta are parallel but opposite in direction, and the second where they are perpendicular and opposite in direction. We calculate and analyze the energy and NMR transition rates for these modes and find that in both cases the finite amplitude dynamics are dominated by a pair of collective states separated by a rotational frequency corresponding to the average moment of inertia.

A novel method inspired by finite volume schemes leverages a cell-average based neural network to solve partial differential equations. By utilizing the maximum and minimum values within a cell to approximate derivatives, one discards local smoothness assumptions, making this approach suitable for hyperbolic and parabolic problems with shocks and boundary layers. A cell-based descriptor is formed by combining the minimum value, maximum value, and cell average to predict solutions at new time steps. Approximation errors are minimized by applying the least squares method, providing an avenue for improving descriptive power and time step prediction. Key advantages of this approach include local adaptivity, cell-based sensitivity, and data efficiency. Comparisons are drawn to conventional finite volume schemes for hyperbolic and parabolic problems, revealing that the cell-based descriptor is particularly valuable for problems involving discontinuities and boundary layers.

The ALICE experiment is designed to conduct in-depth studies of the quark-gluon plasma formed within the Large Hadron Collider and other systems. With the ongoing development of the experiment, ALICE is preparing for LHC Run 3 and potential future runs, during which data processing and detection capabilities will be significantly enhanced. Several key areas of focus involve the integration of large-scale computing systems, a sophisticated particle identification detector, and the implementation of sophisticated scanning and tracking devices.

Our research introduces a method to detect the timelike Unruh effect, a phenomenon where a fast-moving observer perceives quantum vacuum fluctuations as carrying information about spatial locations. A specific measure of this effect, the geometric phase, is shown to be equivalent to the entanglement between forward and backward light cones in spacetime. A new approach for observing the timelike Unruh effect is proposed, and we outline the conditions and steps for a feasible experiment.

One of the most complex tasks in Natural Language Processing, Event Extraction, involves identifying semantically linked event components, typically done in English. We propose a multilingual approach focusing on German, English, and Macedonian, using automatically labeled data from news sources. Our results demonstrate that models can achieve close state-of-the-art performance via knowledge distillation in each language and cross-lingual knowledge distillation of a unified teacher model. Notably, for knowledge distillation in each language, we see only a 1.6% drop in F1 score compared to the combined teacher model, suggesting that further exploration of multilingual pre-training and adaptation techniques could yield even greater improvements.

We examine a complex vector bundle with several levels of structure, defined over a manifold of Calabi-Yau geometry. By projecting this bundle through a surjective and holomorphic function to another geometry, we obtain a new bundle. Our aim is to identify conditions under which this new bundle has positive characteristics, particularly in terms of total Chern forms. This leads us to develop a formula involving the relative Chern classes and relative Segre classes in conjunction with a new, relative push-forward formula for transverse integrals of forms. Specifically, we prove that integrating these forms after projection results in an expression involving the original form's integration and a correction term based on a universal transverse connection and relative Pontryagin classes of a universal family of complex manifolds, specifically a family of smooth surfaces with varying dimensions.

Our detailed analysis of the 256 observations made by the XMM-Newton observatory between 2002 and 2004 provides new insights into the high-energy behavior of the black hole X-ray binary Cyg X-1 during its hard state. By applying the cossim tool, we found significant correlations between pulse phase and energy, revealing two distinct components with different characteristics. These components exhibit different spatial distributions within the source, with their amplitude and phase also varying. Contrary to expectations, the correlations are not more pronounced in the source's softer states but rather diminish as the source transitions into softer states. Furthermore, the Eddington ratio does not appear to influence the correlations. Our findings suggest that the stellar wind from Cyg X-1's companion star can introduce randomised velocity fields in the accretion flow, resulting in observable high-energy temporal and spectral features. Our research indicates that the high-energy component is more affected by the velocity field than the lower-energy component. Our study also provides a complex model of the high-energy spectral and temporal behaviour of Cyg X-1 during its hard state, with a good match between the model and the observed data.

The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, specifically within thermal quantum field theory. By incorporating temperature effects, we derive the non-trivial contributions to the effective potential, thermodynamic parameters, and entropy. Our findings reveal significant impacts on entropy, pressure, and temperature when accounting for the gauge coupling, even at the one-loop order, due to the presence of the non-abelian aether-like terms. Furthermore, we investigate the stability conditions for different non-abelian vector choices and examine their behavior at high temperatures, ultimately aiming to assess the theoretical consistency of this scenario.

Researchers have long sought to bridge the gap between syntax and semantics parsing but so far have had to make a choice between the two. Our approach suggests that simultaneous execution of both tasks can be accomplished using the same neural framework. To test this, we employed the same neural architecture on two different parsing tasks - dependency parsing and role labeling - which utilize the same input sentence representations but produce distinct outputs. As a result, we were able to parse the full SWN corpus in under 10 minutes without any pre-trained models. Our experiments, conducted on three datasets spanning English and Russian, demonstrate that joint parsing can yield equal or better results compared to separate models. Furthermore, we found that adjusting the joint framework by incorporating task-specific components can produce outcomes comparable to a model designed specifically for role labeling.

The observation of short gamma-ray bursts and neutron star mergers has led to renewed interest in understanding the dynamics of postmerger outflows. Low-mass remnant black holes formed from neutron star coalescence, along with surrounding accretion disks, are believed to be a potential source of these outflows. Utilizing special relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations, we have found that magnetohydrodynamic waves in the early postmerger phase can trigger significant disk winds before the remnant black hole forms. These disk winds are highly magnetized and exhibit characteristics consistent with the jets observed in short gamma-ray bursts. Specifically, our simulations indicate that the growth of magnetohydrodynamic waves leads to multiple, brief bursts of disk wind launching within the first 4 milliseconds, lasting up to 10 milliseconds. These bursts are likely caused by the interaction of the magnetosphere with the accretion disk and result in the launching of disk jets. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the postmerger outflows observed in short gamma-ray bursts could be a combination of these disk jets and the magnetospheric outflow that forms the magnetosphere in the first place.

We've analyzed the mass fraction of tidal features in 160,000 early-type galaxies from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program's main sample. This investigation targeted galaxies with masses exceeding 10 to the 11 solar mass mass range between redshifts of 0.1 and 0.4. Our findings show that galaxies with active star formation have a 10 percent higher tidal feature fraction than those without, and we've found tidal features' average light contribution at around 10 percent. Notably, we've discovered a significant correlation between tidal feature fraction and specific star formation rate, noting that star-forming galaxies have the highest tidal feature fractions. This relationship also correlates with line-of-sight velocity dispersion and redshift. Using a model informed by our findings, we've calculated the galaxies' merger rates and found that, on average, a massive galaxy undergoes a merger every 1.5 billion years, and this rate increases by a factor of 1.5 when accounting for tidal features, particularly for galaxies with higher tidal feature fractions. This suggests that tidal features significantly contribute to the galaxies' overall merger rate.

Recent research has revealed that the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation exhibits repulsive gravitational effects. This new outcome is in direct contrast to the well-known attractive nature of gravity according to Newton and Einstein. To further explore this phenomenon, the present study employs a pseudo-Newtonian potential that mirrors the behavior of the field equation in the axisymmetric general relativity. Specifically, circular orbits are used to demonstrate how the region surrounding a mass center transitions from attractive to repulsive when the radius approaches zero. This behavior is shown to be consistent with the repulsive gravity predicted by the theory.

We have obtained deep radio and optical observations of two fast radio bursts, CHydra#1 and CHydra#2, using radio telescopes and optical telescopes. Our observations have placed the most stringent constraints on the occurrence rates of simultaneous optical emission and the delay between radio and optical arrival times for sub-GeV compact objects in low-metallicity extragalactic environments. By analyzing data from CHydra#2, we have ruled out any optical emission with energy of 10^41 ergs in an 8000 au volume within 0.1 seconds of the burst, and have also constrained the occurrence rate of delayed emission with energy of 10^42 ergs in a 10^16 cm zone. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the nature of the energetic compact objects responsible for FRBs. We have also discussed the potential implications of our constraints on the compact object's spin and magnetic field.

The rapid advancement in laser technology design has been fueled by sophisticated design tools that leverage automated design methods, high-performance computing systems, and cutting-edge optical simulation packages. Laser design can be divided into two main approaches: optimization from scratch and reverse engineering, which seeks to replicate high-power lasers already built. Our study demonstrates a successful application of design-by-constraint optimization to create a four-dimensional laser cavity with 1064 nm output and a stable, intrepid mode topology. By combining a detailed ray-tracing model with optical component data, a model-predictive control strategy is developed to simulate and optimize the assembly process, taking into account manufacturing tolerances. Conversely, reverse engineering involves analyzing a cavity's properties to reverse-engineer its parameters, a task made possible with advanced optimization techniques. Our techniques allow us to determine a compact set of essential parameters defining high-power laser cavities, reducing the underlying design space and making optimization more manageable.

Surprisingly, even state-of-the-the models fail to consistently utilize visual inputs when provided. Moreover, it is found that pre-trained language models do not inherently learn to perceive the environment around them, as demonstrated when visually control are made available. We introduce a novel and straightforward technique to incorporate visual controls into text generation by directly connecting visual controls to the existing generation process through an additional head, as well as by adjusting existing generation algorithms.
